#5513. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5512. Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan

Wyld Oaks, a 215-acre mixed-use project in Apopka near Orlando, is underway with 325 apartments starting. The plan totals 6,000 multifamily units, 300,000 SF retail, and major nonresidential uses after a nearly 2-year delay tied to financing constraints.  AI Summary

In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they’ll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with “third spaces,” ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging.

Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida, where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks, where it is building 325 apartment units.

That’s for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes.

Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station.

For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance.

“Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD. “But the option to walk is going to be there.”

With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric.

Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets.

The 215-acre Wyld Oaks community is located in Apopka, a high-growth suburb of Orlando that saw its population grow by roughly 20% between 2020 and 2025. Despite this growth, and the rapid growth of adjacent communities, there remain relatively few walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods for residents and visitors alike.

This need in the market was among the top considerations for Wyld Oaks, which was designed with walkability, livability and community in mind.

“It all starts with density, and trail systems and parks, and having everything closer to one another as opposed to further apart. We have multifamily, and we’re working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.”

All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. Once fully built out, Beninati expects, or at least hopes, that Wyld Oaks will become a top-tier regional destination.

“Economic activity begets economic activity. If you’re bringing your kids to the dentist, that allows you to also maybe do a little grocery shopping. Or if you’re going to work out and you’re with some friends, maybe you’re going to go out and have a drink or supper together. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained.

Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in.

“For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said.

Although Wyld Oaks is primarily multifamily and non-residential, homebuilders could potentially learn lessons from it. The community’s emphasis on third spaces – places that bridge work, home and school – where residents can connect and feel a sense of belonging, could apply just as well to many single-family neighborhoods.

Central Florida, like many other high-growth Sun Belt markets, experienced a post-COVID multifamily building boom. A surge in new construction following the pandemic led to a coinciding surge in new deliveries.

In 2021 and 2022, developers delivered about 8,500 to 8,800 new multifamily units in the Orlando MSA, according to data from Cushman & Wakefield. In 2023 and 2024, the number of deliveries rose to about 12,500 and 13,000, while 2025 saw about 11,000 new units completed.

Like many other Sun Belt markets, this surge in completions oversupplied the market and pressured rents to soften. As a result, financing new multifamily projects in Central Florida became quite challenging by 2024, the reason the first multifamily community at Wyld Oaks was delayed by nearly two years.

According to Beninati, the biggest challenge in the multifamily financing environment in the Orlando market over the past couple of years hasn’t been securing construction loans so much as finding equity investors to fund projects. Investors have grown more discriminating, directing available capital toward established developers with strong track records and projects in desirable locations.

In Wyld Oaks’ case, the developer’s reputation and the project’s location and desirable master plan helped it secure an equity partner, despite the challenging environment.

However, Beninati believes local financing conditions may be starting to improve. A slowdown in new multifamily development over the past couple of years means that the market has become more balanced, and rent power has begun to stabilize. That dynamic could help other multifamily projects become more financially viable.

For Beninati, breaking ground on the community’s first phase was a major milestone, especially after a delay of nearly two years. But it is only a small piece of a much larger vision, and bringing the full community to life will take years, with market conditions shifting along the way. Weathering those changes, Beninati said, comes down to one thing.

“I think it’s just patience. This is a business where you need to be incredibly, incredibly patient,” he said. “It doesn’t just happen overnight. That’s the nature of the real estate business.”

#5511. AVAX NYSE Deal Sparks 10% Rally: Avalanche Wins Tokenized Stock Role

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Avalanche (AVAX) climbed on Tuesday after the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) selected its blockchain technology to power settlement for a new tokenized securities platform. The move gives Avalanche a significant role in Wall Street’s push toward blockchain-based financial infrastructure.

AVAX price reached $8.60, gaining 5.2% over 24 hours. The token had climbed as high as $8.99, putting the psychological $9 resistance level back within reach.

Trading activity also picked up sharply. Avalanche recorded $537 million in 24-hour trading volume, an increase of nearly 448% from the previous day. The announcement followed a rally of as much as 10% on Monday, when AVAX outperformed most major coins.

Avalanche would provide the core ledger technology for the clearing firm supporting NYSE’s upcoming digital alternative trading system (ATS). The platform aims to support 24-hour trading, clearing, and settlement of tokenized securities. Investors could eventually trade tokenized US stocks and exchange-traded funds outside traditional market hours.

Avalanche will provide the underlying blockchain infrastructure through a dedicated network built around institutional requirements. Meanwhile, NYSE will retain its existing Pillar matching engine to process buy and sell orders.

The announcement shows Avalanche’s growing appeal among traditional financial institutions seeking faster and more flexible settlement infrastructure.

The timing is particularly interesting as Wall Street increasingly explores tokenization. Nasdaq is developing its own tokenized securities infrastructure, while the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) is advancing blockchain-based settlement initiatives.

NYSE’s decision gives Avalanche a prominent position in that competition. The exchange operates one of the world’s largest stock markets, making the partnership a significant endorsement of Avalanche’s technology.

AVAX price is approaching a critical technical level after yesterday’s explosive rally. The token climbed from an intraday low near $7.82 toward $8.99, putting $9 within striking distance. A decisive breakout could open the door toward $9.10, the next resistance area.

Trading volume provides another encouraging signal. The sharp increase suggests renewed interest in AVAX as investors react to the NYSE announcement. If buyers maintain momentum above $9, Avalanche could extend its recovery toward higher resistance levels. Conversely, $8 remains the first important psychological support if traders take profits.

The rally also arrives as Avalanche works to strengthen its position in institutional finance. Its blockchain infrastructure is increasingly competing for attention alongside established networks seeking to capture the growing tokenized asset market.

The NYSE announcement gives that narrative considerable weight. Rather than simply attracting another crypto partnership, Avalanche has secured a role in the infrastructure plans of a major traditional stock exchange.

#5510. CoreWeave arrests stock slide after posting a strong earnings beat and raising its full-year guidance

Neocloud infrastructure darling CoreWeave Inc. delivered an impressive revenue beat and raised its full-year guidance today as it demonstrated that demand for artificial intelligence computing remains strong, pushing its stock higher in late trading.

The report comes at a prickly moment for the AI industry as investors increasingly sour on heavily indebted cloud infrastructure startups, while the broader market continues to get to grips with the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

The company reported a third-quarter loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.27 per share, trailing Wall Street’s target of a $1.16 per share loss. But the 168% growth in revenue meant sales came to $3.66 billion, topping expectations of $3.55 billion. All told, CoreWeave reported a net loss in the quarter of $709 million, rising from a $110 million net loss in the same period one year earlier.

Investors may be pleased with CoreWeave’s guidance, though. Company executives said they’re now looking for between $1.275 billion and $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income and $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue for the full year. Wall Street analysts are looking for just $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.86 billion in total sales. CoreWeave’s forecast is notably much higher than the $960 million to $1.15 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in revenue it had forecast three months earlier.

The report was well-received by investors, as CoreWeave’s stock climbed more than 5% in late trading, helping put the brakes on a slide that has seen the company lose more than 40% of its value over the last month. Many investors have sought to abandon stocks that are closely tied to the AI infrastructure buildout amid fears that rising interest rates have made capital much more difficult to come by. Recently, some CoreWeave bond yields have topped 16%.

CoreWeave Chief Executive Michael Intrator (pictured) told analysts on a conference call that most of the company’s capital requirements in fiscal 2027 will be sourced from clients via pre-payments on infrastructure services and from hardware partners such as Nvidia. He added that the company will also seek to raise a “limited amount” in outside funding.

When pressed on this, CoreWeave’s finance chief Nitin Agrawal said the company plans to raise new debt that will be tied to a set of contracts. “At current yields we do not intend to issue additional parent-level unsecured debt through 2027,” he told analysts. “By contrast, the asset-level secured debt market has remained stable, with our loans continuing to trade around par value.”

CoreWeave, along with other neoclouds like Nebius Group N.V., which is set to report its own earnings results on Thursday, has become increasingly reliant on its hardware partner Nvidia as a major benefactor. Nvidia provides CoreWeave with not only the graphics processing units needed to populate its data centers, but also much of the capital it needs to procure those chips.

Eessentially it’s recycling the money it earns throughout the AI economy in order to keep everything ticking over. But investors have become concerned about the long-term viability of what looks like an increasingly circular economy, and Nvidia’s stock has struggled to maintain momentum this year.

With this week’s revelations that Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the chipmaker’s stock has lost almost 10% of its value to start the week. Nvidia’s board of directors has responded by launching an internal investigation, hiring the services of the high-profile legal firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into Huang’s personal life and determine if any company or national security secrets were compromised.

The fallout from that probe will likely have a strong bearing on CoreWeave’s fortunes going forward, as will next week’s widely anticipated initial public offering from AI leader Anthropic PBC. In an update to its IPO prospectus earlier today, the model maker said it’s hoping to achieve a $1.4 trillion valuation through its share sale.

In the meantime, CoreWeave continues to forge ahead with its buildout. During the quarter it said it’s planning to build its first data centers in Asia. It also announced a new cloud-based service called Forge for running and evaluating AI models.

The company said it hopes to have 1.85 gigawatts of active compute power in service by the end of the year, and anticipates its capital expenditure will reach between $37 billion and $39 billion. That’s more or less in line with the Street’s forecast of $37.69 billion in capex this year.

At the end of the quarter, CoreWeave’s total debt was approaching $47 billion. Like its much larger peers in the cloud computing industry, such as Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Oracle Corp., CoreWeave is racing to add more compute capacity to serve its clients.

But there are signs it may struggle to do this in the U.S. Last week, American voters either backed restrictions on data center construction or rejected pro-data center development measures in 40 of 41 states.

Intrator addressed those concerns in the conference call, insisting that he wasn’t overly concerned. “If data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” he said.

In the meantime, CoreWeave continues to see demand for cloud compute escalate, and is now sitting on a massive $132.5 billion revenue backlog, Intrator said. That’s up from just $104 billion three months earlier.

#5509. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5507. Mamdani gives nonprofits first dibs on buying apartment buildings

Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed COPA, requiring owners to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling covered buildings. The law takes effect in 1 year, as a 38 building portfolio with 850 mostly rent stabilized units heads to foreclosure auctions.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed legislation Tuesday giving vetted nonprofits a first shot at buying troubled city apartment buildings.

The new measure arrived too late to spare hundreds of rent-stabilized units from foreclosure, a second loss in Mamdani’s bid to protect such units.

Mamdani ran for office and won on creating and protecting affordable housing. National attention has since focused on his efforts to build more housing and cut red tape. His political inspiration and influence have spread to other parts of the country.

Nithya Raman is a prime example. Under a similar affordability theme, the Los Angeles City Council member, also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ousted an incumbent to become L.A. mayor.

The Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, known as COPA, requires owners of covered buildings to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling. Those groups then get time to make an offer and a right to match a later one. The law takes effect one year after enactment, after the Department of Housing Preservation and Development writes rules.

“This law will give New Yorkers a tool to keep their homes out of the hands of predatory investors seeking to make a quick and easy buck,” Mamdani said at a signing event Tuesday.

He also won in court last week. A Brooklyn appellate panel ruled Nov. 4 that the administration can resume collecting its pied-à-terre tax on high-end second homes, reversing a Staten Island judge who found the rollout flawed. Mamdani says the tax could raise $500 million a year. Other legal challenges remain.

But his administration could not stop the sale of a 38-building portfolio with 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments. Spatial Equity, an affordable housing developer with City Hall’s backing, failed to close a deal to buy the portfolio before an East Harlem auction began Tuesday afternoon.

Had COPA been in effect, a deal like Spatial Equity’s might have followed a defined timeline. Once notified of a sale, qualified groups have 20 days to tell the owner and the Department of Housing Preservation and Development they intend to buy. They then have 70 days to submit a competitive offer.The clock favors the owner if no one steps forward. A property can go to the open market if no group signals interest in the first 20 days. The same goes if the owner rejects every offer by the end of the 70-day window.

Eligible buildings have four or more units and meet at least one test: a year in a city housing enforcement program, an average of three or more hazardous violations per unit, or affordability restrictions under agreements with HPD.

“Those buildings are not just any buildings, Mamdani said. “They are multifamily buildings that have long been victim to pernicious cycles of speculation.”

The 38 buildings belonged to bankrupt Emerald Equities Group. Banks and other institutions that control about $250 million in mortgage loans will foreclose on each building over three auction days.

Lenders rejected Spatial Equity’s initial $68 million bid, according to a City Limits report. They also turned down a $110 million offer last month, tenant leader Cara Polte told Gothamist.

Polte said tenants will keep pushing for a buyer committed to fixing the buildings. Tenants had hoped to turn her building and four others on the block into a community land trust.

A trust managed by several banks and by Sabal Investment Holdings controls the loans. Freddie Mac partially insured them. Sabal has yet to respond to media requests.

Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, said the sale does not end the city’s effort to force owners to improve conditions.

This setback follows Mamdani’s first loss on this front. On Jan. 1, he stood in a Pinnacle-owned building and vowed to take on bad landlords. He then sought a 30-day delay of the bankruptcy auction of Pinnacle’s rent-regulated portfolio, hoping to find a buyer other than Summit Properties USA.

A judge allowed the sale to proceed. Summit won about 5,100 mostly rent-stabilized units from Pinnacle, which had filed for Chapter 11 after Flagstar Bank foreclosed.

Emerald bought the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on stabilized apartments. It took out another $180 million loan in December 2018, six months before state lawmakers passed tenant protections that outlawed many of those tactics.

Lenders foreclosed in 2024. Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later.

A state investigation found Emerald had illegally removed 21 apartments from rent stabilization. The buildings had more than 2,300 housing code violations in April. A retaining wall behind buildings on East 103rd Street collapsed earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Weaver visited in March.

About 1,600 rent-stabilized buildings face financial distress, according to Rent Guidelines Board data. Landlord groups blame rent restrictions, including the board’s two-year rent freeze. Tenant advocates say owners like Emerald borrowed heavily expecting rent increases that later law barred.

In June, Mamdani won a rent freeze through the Rent Guidelines Board for the city’s roughly 1 million stabilized apartments.

Landlords sued to reverse the freeze. The case began in Staten Island, but Justice Ralph Porzio moved it to Manhattan in August, handing Mamdani a partial win. In September, the judge ordered City Hall to turn over communications with the board and signaled he would likely not rule by Oct. 1.

Oct. 1 came and went without a ruling, and the freeze took effect for new and renewing leases.

Meanwhile, a federal lawsuit remains pending over a 2019 state law that limits rents on stabilized units. Small property owners sued in November 2025, arguing the law unconstitutionally keeps stabilized apartments vacant.

COPA’s path was uneven until Mamdani took office. The City Council passed an earlier version in December 2025, but then-Mayor Eric Adams vetoed it, and the Council did not override him. A revised, narrower version passed Oct. 22.

“Progress … is something that we celebrate, and also, we know that it is not inevitable,” Mamdani said. “It has to be won.”

#5506. Higharc, ECI launch MarkSystems integration for big builders

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions launched a MarkSystems integration that syncs 3D home design, options and pricing with ERP workflows, aiming to cut manual data entry, errors and rework for production homebuilders.  AI Summary

Higharc and ECI Software Solutions have released a generally available integration that connects Higharc’s 3D home design and configuration platform with ECI’s MarkSystems ERP for production homebuilders, aiming to cut manual data entry and tighten the link between what is sold and what is built.

The companies announced the launch Nov. 10, saying the jointly developed connection is now available to MarkSystems builders and is already in use at New Home Inc., a Carolinas-based builder that has deployed the integration across its sales and construction operations, according to the announcement.

For many production builders, moving a home from sales to construction requires rekeying pricing, plan configurations and buyer selections across multiple systems and departments. That creates opportunities for discrepancies between sales contracts, purchase orders and what gets built in the field, which can show up as margin erosion, delays and rework.

MarkSystems functions as the system of record for housing production, scheduling and accounting for many small and mid-sized builders. Higharc positions itself as the source of truth for plans, options and the buyer-facing design experience. The integration is designed to let data flow between the two instead of relying on manual handoffs.

“The biggest difference we’re seeing is speed and confidence,” said Matt Riley, owner of New Home Inc., in the announcement. “Our sales team can now sit down with a buyer, configure their home with accurate, up-to-date pricing, and send those selections straight into MarkSystems to write the contract. We’re no longer relying on people to keep information updated in multiple places, where mistakes inevitably happen and we end up absorbing the cost.”

The Higharc–MarkSystems connection is built to close gaps between marketing, sales and operations in a typical production homebuilding workflow. Key capabilities, according to the companies, include:

For builders, this type of connection is aimed at tightening margins and shortening cycle times by eliminating redundant work between sales offices, options studios, purchasing teams and field superintendents. Aligning pricing and configurations across systems can also help reduce surprise variance purchase orders and options that are sold but not built—or built but not paid for.

Production builders have accelerated their adoption of connected ERP, sales and design tools over the past decade, but many still run option pricing, elevations and structural changes through spreadsheets or local databases that do not fully sync with ERP. As build costs and cycle times remain under pressure, misaligned data between sales contracts and job budgets can quickly erode gross margin on a per-lot basis.

By placing Higharc’s 3D, rules-based design engine upstream of MarkSystems and tying the two together, the new integration is trying to turn the plan and option configuration itself into structured data that can feed estimating, purchasing and scheduling. That is a shift from traditional workflows where sales and marketing produce static collateral and construction teams translate that material back into quantities and tasks.

For entry-level and move-up builders running high volumes of similar plans across multiple communities, even small reductions in change orders, option mistakes and rework can compound across hundreds or thousands of closings a year.

Homebuilders can learn more about the integration during ECI Connect, ECI’s customer conference that begins Nov. 16. Representatives from Higharc and ECI plan to be available at the event to discuss how the connection links home design, buyer selections, pricing and construction operations, according to the announcement.

Builders not attending the event can schedule personalized demonstrations with either company.

Higharc describes itself as an AI-driven homebuilding platform for design through construction. The company uses 3D spatial data to generate plans, estimates and construction documents, replacing static plan sets with “live” models that respond to design changes with updated drawings, lot-specific estimates and buyer-facing experiences.

ECI Software Solutions, based in Westlake, Texas, provides cloud-based business software for small and mid-sized businesses in manufacturing, building and construction, field service and distribution. Its portfolio includes ERP, CRM, business intelligence, e-commerce and payment tools, and it serves more than 30,000 customers in over 90 countries, according to the company.

#5505. Camera-Based AI Game Improves Hand Dexterity in Children With Cerebral Palsy, Trial Finds

A peer-reviewed, eight-week randomized trial analyzed data from 45 children, with average adherence of 91.9% in the intervention group.

SEONGNAM, South Korea, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Children with cerebral palsy who practiced hand therapy through an AI-powered game at home for eight weeks showed significantly greater gains on tests of hand dexterity and pinch strength than children who received no intervention, according to a randomized controlled trial published in Disability and Rehabilitation. The program, GemGem400, was developed by GemGem Therapeutics and needs only the camera on a standard smartphone or tablet.

Researchers at Asan Medical Center in Seoul randomly assigned 48 children with cerebral palsy, ages 18 months to 7 years 5 months, and analyzed data from 45. Children in the intervention group trained with GemGem400 for about 15 minutes, three times a week, for eight weeks; the control group received no intervention. The Box and Block Test, the study's primary measure of manual dexterity, improved significantly more in the intervention group in both hands, as did palmar pinch strength in both hands. In the non-dominant hand, scores on the Functional Dexterity Test and tip pinch strength also improved significantly more (p < 0.05 for all).

Children in the intervention group completed their home training with an average adherence of 91.9%, a measure of how consistently they followed the program rather than of treatment success. Caregivers reported high satisfaction with the program and less psychological, time and effort burden. The authors say digital tools like GemGem400 are meant to complement, not replace, in-person occupational therapy, and can support high-repetition hand training at home.

The study was a small, single-center trial with no long-term follow-up. Because the control group received no intervention, the results compare home training with GemGem400 against no added training and do not isolate the effect of the AI technology itself. GemGem founder and CEO Jeklin Kim is a co-author of the paper, and GemGem Therapeutics provided the platform and technical support used in the study.

GemGem400 uses the device's built-in camera to recognize a child's hand and wrist movements in real time and responds with instant visual and audio feedback in the game. Target movements and difficulty can be tailored to each child, so families can continue therapy between clinic visits without gloves, sensors or other hardware.

Kim spent 12 years designing games at Nexon, including MapleStory, before founding GemGem. She is also the mother of a child with cerebral palsy; daily four-hour round trips to her child's therapy, and the uneven quality of care she encountered, led her to build a solution herself.

"Through my own child's rehabilitation journey, I experienced firsthand how difficult it is for families to access consistent, engaging, and effective therapy," said Kim, founder and CEO of GemGem Therapeutics. "We are building a future where every child can receive effective rehabilitation through play, regardless of where they live."

The concept won the 2022 Chung Ju-yung Startup Competition, run by the Asan Nanum Foundation, against a field of 89 applicants per winner. Founded in 2023, GemGem pairs game developers with a pediatric occupational therapist, and its app features licensed Pinkfong content from the company behind "Baby Shark." Kim was named a 2026 Cartier Women's Initiative fellow, representing East Asia. Separately from the Asan Medical Center study, the company is preparing a follow-up study with the University of Utah.

The study, "A novel real-time computer vision and artificial intelligence based hand function rehabilitation program for children with cerebral palsy," was published online Sept. 23, 2026 (DOI: 10.1080/09638288.2026.2735445). Eun Jae Ko of the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, Asan Medical Center, University of Ulsan College of Medicine, is the corresponding author. The research was supported by Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency.

GemGem Therapeutics develops AI-powered, game-based hand rehabilitation for children with cerebral palsy and developmental delays. Its GemGem400 app uses a standard tablet or smartphone camera to track hand movements in real time, letting therapists assign exercises and children complete them through play at home or in clinics and schools. Learn more at gemgem.me/en.

#5504. EDB, Now the Company Behind the Leading Kubernetes Operators for Both Postgres® and ClickHouse® Software, Deepens Its Open Source Commitment

CloudNativePG (CNPG) earns CNCF Incubation, Klio brings near-zero data loss to the project, and the new EDB Postgres AI Plugin for CloudNativePG adds enterprise-grade capabilities.

SALT LAKE CITY, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EnterpriseDB (EDB), the leading sovereign data and AI company, today announced that CloudNativePG (CNPG), the most widely adopted Kubernetes operator for Postgres, created by the company, is now a CNCF Incubating project. The news comes less than a week after EDB completed its acquisition of Altinity, creator of the Altinity Kubernetes Operator for ClickHouse software, uniting two expert teams committed to hardening the world's two leading open source databases for Kubernetes, the foundation global enterprises have standardized on.

During KubeCon North America 2026, EDB also announced its donation of Klio to the CNPG community, giving enterprises running open source Postgres on Kubernetes backup and recovery with near-zero data loss. Ahead of general availability, EDB is previewing two enterprise releases: the EDB distribution of Klio, with certified images, support, and long-term releases; and a new EDB Postgres AI Plugin for CloudNativePG that makes it easy to adopt enterprise features such as transparent data encryption (TDE) to open source CNPG with no operator swap. Together, these milestones give enterprises what they need to run their most critical data on Kubernetes with confidence: independent validation of maturity, protection against data loss, and the freedom to expand with enterprise capabilities without ever leaving open source.

"The open, sovereign future runs on Kubernetes. Never is this more true than in the financial sector, where data agility across transactional and analytical workloads is critical," said Max Romanenko, CTO, EDB. "The increasing investment in agent workforces in banking, finance, and insurance industries makes this even more important than ever before. By continuing to invest and give back across the open source communities behind Postgres, ClickHouse software, and the cloud-native ecosystem, we give enterprises the foundation to build that future at scale, on infrastructure they own and control."

Created in 2019 and open sourced in 2022, CNPG has become the most widely adopted operator that manages the full lifecycle of Postgres clusters on Kubernetes. Customers choose CNPG for portability and automation: The same declarative manifest runs on any cloud or on-premises environment, while self-healing, automated failover, rolling updates, and continuous backup with point-in-time recovery replace manual DBA work and database provisioning. EDB is still its primary maintainer, and extends its own enterprise capabilities to it with EDB Postgres AI for CloudNativePG.

Global enterprises already run CNPG in production, and Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank, manages more than 500 Postgres instances on CNPG. Microsoft's official guide to highly available Postgres on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is built on CNPG.

On November 10, CNCF announced that CNPG has reached Incubation and is the only Postgres operator to do so. This is a significant milestone with vendor-neutral recognition of proven production use, healthy community contributions, and strong governance. Incubation requires stable, versioned APIs and production use that CNCF verifies by interviewing real users of the project. For enterprises looking to operate Postgres across hybrid environments or move critical data to sovereign infrastructure, Incubation is independent confirmation that CNPG runs in production, an important step as enterprises standardize critical workloads on Postgres and Kubernetes.

Klio closes the backup and recovery gaps for CNPG

Near-zero data loss is the bar for any system of record, and until now it has been missing for Postgres on Kubernetes. CNPG's built-in backup options archive Postgres's write-ahead log (WAL) only as completed segments, so an outage can cost up to five minutes of lost transactions. Encryption and disaster recovery depend on infrastructure settings or custom tooling that teams must stitch together themselves. These gaps have kept some of the most critical Postgres workloads off Kubernetes.

EDB built Klio specifically to close those gaps for CNPG and has donated it to the CNPG community. Instead of archiving WAL files in completed segments, Klio streams WAL continuously. While other recovery solutions pull every piece of data back from remote storage, Klio keeps a local copy next to your cluster, so restores run at disk speed and avoid the cost of pulling a full copy from storage on every request.

Klio encrypts customers' data in transit and at rest, using rotatable keys that you control. Klio also lets you choose where your backups live: on local volumes, in the S3-compatible storage you pick for disaster recovery, or both. One Klio server can protect many clusters and shows the health of each backup in one place.

Two operators, two databases, one data layer

More than half of Postgres users already run or are considering ClickHouse software. EDB and Altinity now arrive at KubeCon as one company, bringing the two together in one multi-model data layer, EDB Postgres AI (PG AI), running natively on Kubernetes, as open source, in the customer's own environment.

The Altinity Kubernetes Operator, maintained since 2019 and pulled more than 108 million times from Docker Hub, was the first Kubernetes operator built for real-time analytics. Its design reflects how ClickHouse software scales: It models clusters as shards of peer replicas that all accept writes, runs ClickHouse Keeper as its own managed resource for coordination, and rolls restarts shard by shard while distributed tables route queries around an unavailable replica, so operations proceed without downtime.

Both operators follow the same Kubernetes pattern, declarative resources reconciled in a loop, while doing very different work inside it. That shared pattern is the basis for running both under one control plane, so a team can keep payments on Postgres, run fraud analytics on ClickHouse software fed by change data capture (CDC), and manage both with one operating model and one support relationship. EDB plans to introduce integrated enterprise ClickHouse capabilities in Q4 2026.

At KubeCon, EDB Chief Architect Todd Willey and Altinity CEO Robert Hodges are recording "Two Operators, Two Databases," an upcoming episode of The New Stack podcast on running Postgres and ClickHouse software on Kubernetes.

From open source to enterprise, with no operator swap

At KubeCon, EDB is also previewing two enterprise offerings, both planned for general availability by the end of 2026: an EDB distribution of Klio, with certified images, enterprise support, and long-term-support releases; and an EDB Postgres AI Plugin for CloudNativePG, which makes it easy to add enterprise features such as transparent data encryption to open source CNPG with no operator swap. Community images stay free.

EDB Postgres AI (PG AI) is the sovereign AI data system for the agentic enterprise. Built on Postgres, the world's leading open source database, PG AI unifies transactional, analytical, and AI workloads in a single architecture, eliminating the data movement, ETL, and operational fragmentation that slow enterprises down. With governance enforced at the data layer and the flexibility to deploy on-premises, in hybrid environments, or across clouds, enterprises operationalize their data and AI on infrastructure they own and controlâreaching production-ready sovereign AI in weeks, not months. As one of the most active contributors to the PostgreSQL project, EDB is deeply invested in the vitality of the global open source community. To learn more, visit www.enterprisedb.com.

#5503. Reverse mortgage leaders on alleviating sales and referral pain points

Presenters at NRMLA’s Annual Convention discussed practical tactics for a rate-sensitive reverse mortgage market, from LESA reduction and insurance shopping to borrower communication. They also stressed using partner introductions, explaining line-of-credit growth and leveraging CRMP training.  AI Summary

The National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) kicked off its Annual Convention & Expo on Tuesday in San Antonio with some practical advice for originators who are looking to close more deals in a rate-sensitive environment.

Reverse mortgage production has shifted in 2026 as the majority of borrowers are now using proprietary products rather than federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). But regardless of the product being used, experts stressed creative problem-solving, proactive communication, financial planner relationships and next-level education as ways for loan officers to distinguish themselves in a difficult market.

Dan Hultquist, co-founder of REVERSE plus and director of reverse mortgage communications at Movement Mortgage, focused his presentation on transactions that are short to close — when the proceeds don’t cover the required payoffs and closing costs.

Common reasons why a borrower needs to bring more money to the table include lower principal limit factors tied to higher mortgage rates, borrowers who have refinanced repeatedly and the required life expectancy set-aside (LESA) for HECMs. He advised loan officers to consider different solutions for the level of severity.

When borrowers are short to close by a small amount like a few thousand dollars, a potential solution is to schedule their closing within six months of the borrower’s next birthday, so they “age up” and qualify for additional proceeds and/or a smaller LESA.

For borrowers who are short to close by a larger amount, shifting from a HECM to a proprietary loan or a second-lien product can make more sense as it eliminates the need for an upfront mortgage insurance premium. Additionally, the LO might look to persuade the borrower to dip into their retirement savings or obtain gift funds from a relative, since the elimination of the monthly mortgage payment may help them recover that sum over time.

Hultquist said he’s seen deals that are short to close by more than $100,000 saved in this fashion.

When a borrower is short to close specifically because of the LESA, property tax exemptions may provide a way forward. With HECM transactions, Hultquist noted that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) does not have a flat discount on taxable assets. While 15% is the default discount, the client’s actual tax rate can be used, potentially saving money.

Shopping for a new homeowners insurance policy with a lower deductible should also be looked at. “Your insurance company, they know that seniors don’t shop. Guess what happens to their insurance premiums every year? They keep going up until they shop,” Hultquist remarked.

John Luddy, senior vice president at Supreme Lending, has spent 25-plus years exclusively originating reverse mortgages. Over the course of thousands of conversations, he’s identified some key questions to ask of borrowers, spouses and lead sources at the start of the transaction.

The first question Luddy asks every client is, “How did you get my name?” The answer can tell him whether paid advertising campaigns are working.

“Advertising is the empty well that will take as many buckets of your money as you want to put into it,” he said. “You might feel good seeing your name on the marquee somewhere, but if it’s not drawing results, you’re wasting money.”

The same question also helps him identify who to call if a borrower stalls. Many clients, Luddy said, hesitate before closing as they look for an alternative. But lead sources like attorneys, financial planners or accountants “can be a little bolder” in their interactions than an originator, so they may be able to nudge the client across the finish line.

With lead sources, Luddy’s key question is, “What can I do to earn your business?” Real estate agents, for example, want their phone calls to be returned and for the LO to demonstrate deep product knowledge, while financial planners want any loan to fit into their existing strategy with a client.

Banks that don’t offer reverse mortgages can be a rich source of leads due to customers who are denied for other types of credit. And Luddy said bank branch managers will send repeat referral business if there’s no surprises in the reverse mortgage process.

He also urged the audience to consider borrower disabilities, such as hearing loss, as a potential hurdle.

“If they were a veteran, if they worked in manufacturing, if they worked in construction, or if they’re over 62, they may be suffering from hearing loss,” he said. “They’re not going to feel comfortable moving forward if they only understand every third word.”

Ryan Ponsford of Equity Wealth Academy, who’s well known to the NRMLA audience, argued that psychology matters more than math in reverse mortgage sales, even when dealing with financial advisers to capture more business.

Originators should discuss voluntary payments and the lack of a prepayment penalty for reverse mortgages. This gives borrowers a better sense of control over their financial responsibilities.

When speaking with business partners, don’t ask for referrals, which Ponsford called “transactional.” Instead, ask for introductions.

“An introduction is different than a referral because an introduction done right is a transfer of trust. Somebody that is trusted is transferring their trust to you,” he explained.

Financial advisers, he said, should leave conversations with an understanding that reverse mortgages apply to more people than they realize and that homeowners should consider them earlier in life.

Ponsford recommended three questions to ask advisers when attempting to forge a referral relationship.

And while psychology means a lot, it doesn’t mean everything. For example, the compounding growth feature of a reverse mortgage line of credit is essential for LOs to comprehend before they approach advisers. “If you can’t explain how line-of-credit growth works, you’re a nonstarter in the financial solutions industry,” Ponsford said.

Scott Harmes, national manager of reverse at C2 Financial — and his daughter Christina Harmes of Barrett Financial — are on the short list of Certified Reverse Mortgage Professionals (CRMPs), a designation earned through industry experience, a letter of recommendation and passing a complex exam.

He originated his first reverse mortgage about 16 years ago for the parents of a previous client, a deal that “changed their lives, and it changed mine,” he said. He stopped doing traditional forward mortgages about eight years ago to focus solely on reverse,

Harmes said he passed the CRMP exam on his first try and later built a detailed study guide for his colleagues to use that resulted in a “virtually 100%” pass rate. The designation, he said, has helped him to solidify more referral partnerships, to the point where he said he rarely loses deals except for when retail shops offer pricing he can’t match.

At C2 Financial, Harmes has constructed a mentorship model in which an experienced LO and a novice LO work together on three reverse mortgage files, with the trainee gaining additional responsibilities with each file. After that, they’ve typically gained enough knowledge to do the work on their own.

When it comes to borrower education, Harmes stressed that the process works best when information is offered in bite-sized chunks, rather than loan proposals accompanied by dozens of pages. Counseling is a key part of that process and there are pitfalls to be aware of.

“My policy is, I never tell them to look for a free session or a session paid for by a grant, because honestly, I think that’s too much work. We’re (sometimes) giving them three pages of counselors. I don’t want them dialing for dollars for four hours,” Harmes said.

“I originate in California, and there’s a state law that you can’t order the appraisal or any services that would cost the borrower until the eighth day after counseling. So we want to get that counseling session as soon as possible.”

#5502. Dreeze launches with $33M to recover entire cloud applications, not just their data

Israeli cloud application recovery startup Dreeze Inc. formally launched today with $33 million in new funding to bring what it calls Application Revival to enterprises running workloads in the public cloud.

Dreeze provides software aimed at what happens after a backup has done its job. Cloud-native applications depend on infrastructure, identities and secrets as well as data, and all of it has to come back in the right order before an application will run.

The company calls the manual work that follows a “recovery scramble.” Searching for credentials and rebuilding connections by hand can keep an application down for days or weeks after its data is restored.

Preparation starts well before an outage, when Dreeze’s software traces each cloud resource and dependency back to the application that relies on it. Its recovery plan comes from what is actually running, and changes to the environment update it automatically.

Configuration files, keys and application data go into an immutable, air-gapped vault, which customers can replicate across regions. When an outage hits, Dreeze rebuilds those pieces, plus the infrastructure and identities around them, in dependency order. Teams can also rehearse the full plan ahead of time as an automated test that ends with a working copy of the application, and production is left alone while it runs.

Getting the data back “doesn’t mean the business is back,” co-founder and Chief Executive Ziv Kedem said. With cyberattacks increasing, he said, enterprises need to plan on the basis that a critical application will go down at some point.

Jeremy Miller, founder and chief executive of Denver-based technology consulting firm Coravant LLC, said his firm wanted to work with Dreeze “from the start.” Most of its customers can back up public cloud data without much trouble, he said. Their worry is restarting a whole application with every dependency in sequence.

Dreeze is the third recovery company from Kedem and his brother Oded Kedem, its chief technology officer. The pair sold Kashya Inc. to EMC Corp. in 2006. Zerto Ltd., the disaster recovery software company they started in 2009, went to Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. for $374 million in 2021. Avi Raichel, Dreeze’s third co-founder, became Zerto’s chief operating officer that year, shortly before the sale.

Norwest Venture Partners and Bessemer Venture Partners led the seed round. Claltech also participated. Dreeze employs 70 people across Israel and the U.S. and plans to put the money into product development and a larger sales and marketing team.

Few teams understand the recovery problem “as deeply as this one,” Norwest General Partner Dror Nahumi said. In a blog post, Bessemer said Dreeze uses artificial intelligence to work out how thousands of cloud resources connect to the applications they serve. That picture shifts with every change, including ones made by AI agents.

Dreeze’s software is generally available now for Amazon Web Services Inc. customers. A version for Microsoft Corp.’s Azure is in early access, with general availability planned for early next year.

#5501. GLOBAL MANUFACTURERS ACCELERATE STOCKPILING TO MITIGATE FUTURE INFLATION AND SHORTAGES: GEP GLOBAL SUPPLY CHAIN VOLATILITY INDEX

CLARK, N.J., Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GEP Global Supply Chain Volatility Index, a leading indicator tracking demand conditions, shortages, transportation costs, inventories and backlogs, based on a monthly survey of 27,000 businesses, showed that manufacturers accelerated precautionary stockpiling in October, reflecting growing concerns about future inflation and supply disruptions.

The increase was particularly pronounced in North America, where the safety stockpiling indicator more than doubled from September, and Europe, where inventory building rebounded sharply.

This signals that manufacturers are purchasing additional materials to protect production against higher future costs and potential shortages, even as the pace of global purchasing growth moderates.

While this inventory buildup may support manufacturing activity in the near term, it also ties up working capital and creates a risk of weaker purchasing demand once companies have accumulated sufficient stock.

Meanwhile, global transportation costs increased for the second consecutive month, adding to already high inflationary pressures here.

Despite these concerns, global manufacturing activity remained resilient. Purchasing demand continued to grow, supported by sustained strength across Asia and improving European demand. However, overall global supply chain pressures eased in October as material and labor shortages declined.

"Manufacturers are increasingly concerned about what's ahead, particularly inflation and the risk of renewed supply disruptions," said John Piatek, Vice President, Consulting, GEP. "They're responding by building larger inventory buffers to protect production and manage future costs.  The concern is what happens next. This additional purchasing is supporting manufacturing activity today, but it also ties up working capital. Once inventories are built, purchasing could slow, creating a drag on manufacturing and the wider economy in 2027."

Interpreting the data:Index > 0, supply chain capacity is being stretched. The further above 0, the more stretched supply chains are.Index < 0, supply chain capacity is being underutilized. The further below 0, the more underutilized supply chains are.
