#5500. A military spouse’s advice for serving veteran homebuyers

Mortgage teams can better serve veteran homebuyers through VA loan education and community support. Veterans move often, and 34% had service-connected disabilities in 2025.   AI Summary

During my husband’s active duty, our family lived in five different states. We packed up our belongings 10 times, rented several homes and purchased two. We learned how to settle into a new place quickly, but making a house feel permanent was another matter.

Knowing another move was likely around the corner, we sometimes questioned whether decorating, or even unpacking, was worth the effort. It was difficult to feel connected to our neighbors and community when we knew we would eventually have to start over.

That repeated disruption is familiar to many military families. According to the Military Family Advisory Network, military families move, on average, every 2.5 years.

After more than two decades as a military spouse and, more recently, a veteran spouse, I know that finding a home is only one part of the transition from military to civilian life. A veteran may be looking for civilian work while learning to live with service-related health challenges. Their spouse may be rebuilding a career interrupted by repeated moves. Children have their own adjustments to make.

As mortgage professionals, we often meet families during this transition and have a window into some of the pressures and uncertainty they might be facing. As part of our mission of making home happen, we can also help our organizations and colleagues understand some of the unique circumstances surrounding these families and where we can collectively provide more assistance.

In August 2025, 5.8 million veterans, or 34% of all U.S. veterans, had a service-connected disability, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. For some families, access to health care may be a pressing concern. Others may need help finding work or support for a spouse or child. Mortgage lenders and other employers can contribute through organizations equipped to address those needs.

Begin by getting to know the organizations already serving military families. For example, Camp Hope provides a residential program addressing combat-related trauma, along with support for families, at no cost. Stronghold Food Pantry provides free food assistance to military families, while InDependent Wellness offers wellness resources and programs for military spouses. Ask these organizations where support is most needed before deciding what to offer. Some organizations may benefit most from a financial contribution; others may need volunteers or help reaching families who could use their services.

Employers have opportunities within their own workplaces, too. They can take action by investing in training and career opportunities for transitioning service members and veterans. The Department of War (DoW) SkillBridge program offers industry training and work experience to service members with 180 days or fewer remaining before military discharge. Becoming a program provider is one way an employer can help service members prepare for civilian careers. Employee resource groups can also give veterans a place to connect with colleagues and help others understand their experiences.

The VA home loan benefit gives eligible veterans an important financing option. According to the National Association of REALTORS®, 55% of veteran homebuyers in 2025 used VA financing. Helping a family evaluate that option requires mortgage professionals who know the program well enough to explain how it applies to their circumstances.

That requires ongoing education for loan officers and broker partners. For example, mortgage professionals should understand that the benefit is not limited to one use and that eligible borrowers may qualify for another VA-backed loan while an existing one remains active.

Lenders can put that education into practice through regular in-person or virtual training and digital resources that address program requirements and borrower questions. Mortgage originators should take advantage of those resources and guidance from the VA, rather than rely on assumptions about who can qualify. A thorough understanding of the program can help them identify options they might otherwise overlook.

The conversation should begin with a question about whether the borrower has served. From there, ask what is prompting the move and how the purchase fits their finances. Take time to understand what the family needs from the home and whether the payments will be manageable. Evaluate VA financing alongside other appropriate options so the borrower can make an informed choice.

For veterans and their families transitioning to civilian life, a permanent home can mean an end to planning around the next move. It offers the chance to build lasting connections with neighbors and become part of a community.

For our family, my husband’s service-connected disabilities and our son’s special needs have made a stable home especially important as we adjust to life after the military. I know how much it means to finally have a place where you can unpack everything, settle in and make a home your own. Finding the additional support our family needs has been part of that adjustment, too.

I still think about those moving boxes and all the times our family had to begin again. This Veterans Day, it’s my hope that employers will look at how they support military families in their communities and workplaces. Mortgage professionals can examine whether their knowledge is keeping pace with the needs of the borrowers they serve.

For those working with borrowers, one place to start is a 30-minute commitment: Study one VA guideline you don’t fully understand and learn about one aspect of military family life. Make that a starting point for ongoing learning about both the benefit and the people who use it.

Our family needed a home we could settle into. We also needed people who understood what we were adjusting to. We owe it to veterans and their families to learn about the challenges they face after military service. To honor their service to our country, we as individuals and organizations should take every opportunity to serve them too.

Brittany Boccher is the Newrez National Director of Military Strategy & Military Engagement.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5499. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5498. GLOBAL MANUFACTURERS ACCELERATE STOCKPILING TO MITIGATE FUTURE INFLATION AND SHORTAGES: GEP GLOBAL SUPPLY CHAIN VOLATILITY INDEX

CLARK, N.J., Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- GEP Global Supply Chain Volatility Index, a leading indicator tracking demand conditions, shortages, transportation costs, inventories and backlogs, based on a monthly survey of 27,000 businesses, showed that manufacturers accelerated precautionary stockpiling in October, reflecting growing concerns about future inflation and supply disruptions.

The increase was particularly pronounced in North America, where the safety stockpiling indicator more than doubled from September, and Europe, where inventory building rebounded sharply.

This signals that manufacturers are purchasing additional materials to protect production against higher future costs and potential shortages, even as the pace of global purchasing growth moderates.

While this inventory buildup may support manufacturing activity in the near term, it also ties up working capital and creates a risk of weaker purchasing demand once companies have accumulated sufficient stock.

Meanwhile, global transportation costs increased for the second consecutive month, adding to already high inflationary pressures here.

Despite these concerns, global manufacturing activity remained resilient. Purchasing demand continued to grow, supported by sustained strength across Asia and improving European demand. However, overall global supply chain pressures eased in October as material and labor shortages declined.

"Manufacturers are increasingly concerned about what's ahead, particularly inflation and the risk of renewed supply disruptions," said John Piatek, Vice President, Consulting, GEP. "They're responding by building larger inventory buffers to protect production and manage future costs.  The concern is what happens next. This additional purchasing is supporting manufacturing activity today, but it also ties up working capital. Once inventories are built, purchasing could slow, creating a drag on manufacturing and the wider economy in 2027."

Interpreting the data:Index > 0, supply chain capacity is being stretched. The further above 0, the more stretched supply chains are.Index < 0, supply chain capacity is being underutilized. The further below 0, the more underutilized supply chains are.

#5497. If you own the asset, you should own the project data

Owners often inherit thousands of closeout files but lose decision context stored in contractor systems. A persistent owner-controlled record improves operations, diligence, portfolio learning and future AI analysis.   AI Summary

Real estate owners spend years making decisions before a shovel hits the ground, then decades living with the consequences of those decisions after construction is complete. Yet during construction, something unusual often happens: The most complete version of the project can end up living inside systems controlled by a project team whose role is temporary.

That is not an argument against general contractors or the technology they use. Contractors need their own systems to execute the work — to manage RFIs, submittals, drawings, schedules, changes, commitments, field activity and the hundreds of other workflows required to deliver a project. The issue is what happens to all of that information when the project ends.

For the owner, construction is only one chapter in a much longer relationship with the asset, and the information created during that chapter should remain just as durable as the building itself.

By the time a general contractor mobilizes, an owner may already have spent months or years developing the project. There has been an investment thesis, underwriting, capital planning, site diligence, entitlements, early budgeting, design development, consultant coordination, procurement decisions, lender requirements and investor approvals.

Each of these steps creates information and, more importantly, context: why one design option was selected over another, why the budget moved, which assumptions drove the underwriting, which risks were identified early and which decisions were deferred into construction.

Then the project moves into delivery, and the volume of information accelerates. Drawings are revised, RFIs are answered, submittals are reviewed, contracts are executed, schedules change, pay applications are processed and change orders are negotiated. Decisions are documented across meetings, email, project-management software and individual files.

When construction ends, the asset’s operating life continues. The asset moves into operations, warranties begin to matter, capital projects follow, systems get replaced, spaces are renovated and new teams inherit the property. The asset may later be refinanced, sold or redeveloped. The asset’s history needs to remain accessible through changes in project teams, operating staff and ownership. The way that history is maintained should reflect that reality.

During construction, it is completely reasonable for the general contractor to operate its own project-management environment; in many cases, that is where the day-to-day execution record is most complete. The problem begins when that environment also becomes the owner’s only durable record of what happened.

At turnover, owners can receive thousands of files — drawings, warranties, manuals, RFIs, submittals, schedules, photos, meeting records and closeout documents. Technically, the information was transferred, but information and usable history are not always the same thing.

A folder can tell you what the final drawing was; it may not tell you why the design changed. A change-order file can tell you what was approved; it may not clearly preserve the sequence of decisions that created the change. A final budget can tell you where the project landed; it may not preserve how the forecast evolved along the way.

The distinction matters because the value of project information is not simply in possessing the files. It is in maintaining enough structure and context to understand what happened and why. When that continuity breaks at turnover, the next team has to reconstruct the story.

The answer is not for owners to dictate every piece of software used by every project participant — that would create a different problem. General contractors, architects, engineers, consultants and trade partners all have tools and workflows that support their roles, and those systems are important to project execution and should continue to be.

What the owner needs instead is a persistent layer of information that remains under its control throughout the asset lifecycle. That record should begin before construction, remain active while the project is being delivered and continue after turnover. During construction, information can move between the owner’s environment and the systems used by the project team through workflows, integrations, APIs, exports or agreed reporting processes.

In practice, that means being able to access, export and reuse the agreed project record without depending on a former project participant’s account. Owners should define the required records, their format and responsibility for maintaining them before delivery begins.

The goal is not to duplicate every click made inside a contractor’s software. It is to make sure the information that matters to the long-term owner does not disappear when the temporary project organization dissolves.

Not everything created during construction has equal long-term value. The enduring record should focus on the information required to understand how the asset became what it is.

That starts with the financial history: approved budgets, commitments, forecast changes, contingency usage, major cost movements and the financial impact of significant project decisions. It also includes the decision history — major approvals, design changes, scope decisions, responsible parties and the supporting information behind those decisions.

Then there is the technical project record: drawings, specifications, RFIs, submittals, schedule information and other documentation that explains what was designed and ultimately built. Finally, there is the turnover record — as-builts, warranties, manuals, punch and closeout documentation and the information future teams will need to operate, maintain or modify the asset.

The important point is not the specific software used to store each item. It is continuity. Five years after completion, someone working on the property should be able to understand the decisions made five years earlier without starting an archaeological dig through old inboxes, shared drives and archived contractor accounts.

Construction information is often treated as though its usefulness peaks at closeout. For owners, the opposite may be true. A complete development and construction history can become increasingly useful as the asset ages: operations teams can use it to understand equipment, warranties and design intent and asset managers can use it when evaluating future capital work.

The same history also supports investment and portfolio decisions. Development teams can compare budgets, scopes and outcomes against previous projects, and executives can benchmark performance across a portfolio. Future project teams can understand why earlier decisions were made instead of repeating the same analysis, and the information can also support underwriting, refinancing and disposition diligence by making the history of the asset easier to understand.

This becomes even more valuable for owners with multiple properties. One project record is useful; a consistent record across 20, 50 or 100 assets begins to create institutional knowledge. Patterns become visible, assumptions can be tested, budget performance can be compared and recurring problems can be identified — lessons learned on one project can actually influence the next one. The organization’s experience stops resetting every time a project team changes.

Artificial intelligence makes this conversation more important, but not because every owner needs an AI strategy for every construction workflow today. The larger issue is much simpler: AI becomes more useful when it has access to complete, structured and trustworthy information.

An owner might want to understand why similar scopes repeatedly generated changes, how contingency usage varied across developments or which underwriting assumptions proved wrong. Answering those questions requires more than a collection of final documents; it requires a traceable history of decisions and outcomes.

If each project’s information is fragmented across contractor platforms, consultant systems, shared drives, inboxes and archived files, an AI model faces the same problem a human does: the information may technically exist, but reconstructing the story becomes difficult. The owners that preserve a consistent project history today are not simply improving document retention — they are building the information base from which future analysis becomes possible.

There is an important distinction between controlling a project and controlling the enduring record of a project. Owners do not need every contractor to abandon the systems that help them build effectively, and they do not need to centralize every workflow or capture every administrative action performed during construction. What they do need is continuity over the information that explains the asset they ultimately own.

The owner owns the building. It carries the financial consequences of the decisions made during development, operates the asset after the project team leaves, funds the next capital program, and answers the questions of the next lender, investor, buyer or development team. The information describing how that asset was conceived, financed, designed, built and changed should be treated accordingly.

Construction teams move on, and ownership can change. The project record should remain with the asset, available to the people responsible for its future.

Adam Stark is a Special Forces veteran and construction technology executive with experience spanning development, project delivery, construction management and operational systems in the built world.  This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5495. AMD introduces Epyc 6 processors for AI agent workloads

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. today debuted a new line of central processing units for servers.

The Epyc 6 series, which is also known as Venice, comprises 10 CPUs that are organized into two groups. The first set includes chips with a large number of relatively slow cores. The remaining CPUs feature fewer, higher-frequency cores.

Both chip collections feature optimizations designed to speed up artificial intelligence agents. AI agents run their neural networks on graphics cards and use CPUs to power their tools, the applications with which they carry out work.

CPUs also perform certain other tasks in machine learning clusters. According to AMD, Epyc 6 chips can support up to 3.3 more agents per watt than Nvidia Corp.’s Vera CPU. Additionally, the company says that its processor series significantly outperforms comparable Intel Corp. silicon.

Deploying an AI agent’s tools on CPUs with a relatively small core count can reduce software expenses in some cases. Certain enterprise applications, notably databases, are billed according to the number of cores on which they run. As a result, deploying a database on one high-frequency core is cheaper than using two slower ones that together provide the same amount of processing power.

The two highest frequency Epyc 6 chips have a base speed of 4.05 gigahertz. They can boost their clock to 5.3 GHz when running demanding workloads. Both chips have 96 cores and a 384-megabyte cache.

The two densest Epyc 6 chips, meanwhile, include 256 cores with a base speed of 2.55 GHz. Each core can power two threads, or stream of calculations, for a total of 512 threads. That enables the chips to run a large number of AI agents at once. Some large language models spin up hundreds of agents or more when tackling complex tasks.

The Epyc 6 series is based on a new core architecture called Zen 6. Its IPC, a key measure of CPU performance, is 31% higher than AMD’s previous design when running AI workloads. The increase partly stems from the fact that AMD uses Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s latest two-nanometer node to make Zen 6 cores.

The cores come in two editions. There’s a version called simply Zen 6 that is optimized for clock speed and a scaled-down edition, Zen 6c, that is designed to power CPUs with high core counts. Zen 6c core features an enhanced out-of-order processing mechanism not included in the standard edition. The mechanism speeds up programs by performing some calculations well before the results are needed.

Zen 6 also includes AI-specific optimizations. The architecture is compatible with the FP16 data format, which makes it possible to lower agents’ hardware footprint by compress the information they process. There’s also improved support for VNNI-INT8, a technology that condenses multiple AI calculations into a single operation to save time.

“AI is significantly expanding the role of the CPU across every layer of the data center,” said Dan McNamara, the senior vice president and general manager of AMD’s Compute and Enterprise AI unit. “With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, customers can standardize on the proven x86 foundation while choosing a workload-optimized solution to run more agents.”

AMD says that a number of major data center suppliers have already started shipping servers equipped with Epyc 6 chips. Additionally, the processors power a pair of Microsoft Azure instances optimized for AI inference workloads and chip design software.

#5494. Winning in a buyer’s market

With inventory rising and pending sales hitting historic lows, today's buyers have leverage they haven't seen in years. Jennifer Beeston breaks down three common client hesitations—high rates, high prices and closing costs—and outlines how agents and lenders can use seller concessions and buydowns to get deals across the finish line.   AI Summary

As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America.

Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable. It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales!

Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates?  Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies.

Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate.  I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there.

Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay.  It is up to the seller to say yes or no.

Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that’s a missed opportunity.  The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer.  Write the offer.

Did you know many buyers don’t realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller’s market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer’s market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays.

As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes?  No, but that is the beauty of the buyer’s market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it.

Jennifer Beeston is the EVP of National Sales at Chairman’s Circle (NMLS ID: 247743). This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5493. DFRobot HUSKYLENS 2 AI Vision Sensor Wins Teach Awards 2026 in the EdTech & Software Category for Secondary

SHANGHAI, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DFRobot's HUSKYLENS 2 AI vision sensor has been named the winner in the EdTech & Software Category for Secondary at the Teach Awards.

The Teach Awards, organised by Teachwire, recognise education technology products, resources and projects that deliver real value in teaching and learning. Judging focuses on practical classroom impact, ease of use, and the difference a product makes to students' learning experience. The award for HUSKYLENS 2 reflects recognition of its value in secondary-level AI and STEM teaching.

HUSKYLENS 2 is DFRobot's second-generation AI vision sensor, designed for education and maker scenarios. It features more than 20 built-in AI models, an on-board touchscreen interface, support for training and deploying custom models, and compatibility with mainstream open-source hardware platforms. The product is designed to lower the barrier to learning artificial intelligence, enabling students to complete AI vision projects â such as object recognition, face recognition and line following â without first mastering complex programming, turning abstract AI concepts into classroom practice that students can observe, operate and verify.

#5490. Caris Launches Landmark Study to Challenge Fragmented Testing in Myeloid Malignancies

First patients enrolled in prospective, multi-institutional study evaluating whether a single Whole Genome Sequencing workflow can replace conventional cytogenetics, FISH and targeted NGS testing

IRVING, Texas, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Caris Life SciencesÂ® (Caris), a leading next-generation AI TechBio company, today announced that the first patients have been enrolled in a prospective, real-world observational study evaluating Caris ChromoSeqâ¢, a Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) assay designed to provide comprehensive genomic characterization of myeloid malignancies through a single integrated workflow. The first patients enrolled in late September 2026, marking the start of prospective evidence generation for the assay.

The study represents a significant milestone in Caris' effort to simplify one of the most fragmented molecular testing paradigms in oncology. Approximately 300 adult patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) will be enrolled across multiple U.S. institutions through July 2027.

For decades, clinicians have relied on a combination of cytogenetics, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) to characterize myeloid malignancies. This multi-test approach often requires coordination across multiple laboratories and platforms, creating delays, administrative complexity, and the challenge of integrating separate test results into a single clinical interpretation.

Caris ChromoSeq leverages Whole Genome and Whole Transcriptome Sequencing to deliver high-resolution genomic profiling in a single integrated report with a turnaround time of approximately seven days. The prospective study will evaluate how this comprehensive approach performs in routine clinical practice compared with conventional testing methods across key measures including risk stratification, ease of use, and turnaround time.

"Oncology has embraced comprehensive molecular profiling, yet patients with myeloid malignancies are often still evaluated through a fragmented testing process that requires multiple assays and workflows," said David Spetzler, MS, PhD, MBA, President of Caris Life Sciences. "Caris ChromoSeq was developed to challenge that paradigm. This study is designed to generate the real-world evidence needed to demonstrate how a single Whole Genome Sequencing workflow can provide a more comprehensive and efficient approach to molecular characterization."

The scientific foundation for Whole Genome Sequencing in myeloid malignancies has already been established. Research published in The New England Journal of Medicine demonstrated that Whole Genome Sequencing can support diagnosis and risk stratification in patients with AML and MDS. However, despite these advances, adoption in routine clinical practice remains limited.

The Caris ChromoSeq study is intended to address the next critical question: how a Whole Genome Sequencing based workflow performs in real-world clinical settings across diverse institutions and patient populations.

The study, "An observational study to describe the performance of Caris ChromoSeq as compared to conventional cytogenetics, FISH, and NGS testing among patients receiving the Caris ChromoSeq assay for hematologic malignancies" (NCT07680868), received Institutional Review Board approval on April 23, 2026. The first patients began enrollment in late September 2026.

The start of patient enrollment follows MolDX approval of Caris ChromoSeq and marks another important milestone in Caris' strategy to expand access to Whole Genome Sequencing while generating the prospective clinical evidence necessary to support broader adoption.

About Caris ChromoSeqCaris ChromoSeqâ¢ is a Whole Genome and Whole Transcriptome Sequencing assay designed for the comprehensive genomic characterization of myeloid malignancies, including acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and myeloproliferative neoplasms. By consolidating genomic analysis into a single integrated workflow and report, Caris ChromoSeq is designed to simplify traditionally fragmented testing approaches while delivering clinically relevant molecular insights for diagnosis, risk stratification and patient management.

About Caris Life Sciences Caris Life SciencesÂ® (Caris) is a leading TechBio company actively developing and commercializing innovative solutions to transform healthcare. Through comprehensive molecular profiling (Whole Genome, Whole Exome and Whole Transcriptome Sequencing), advanced AI and machine learning, Caris has created the large-scale, multimodal clinico-genomic database and computing capability needed to analyze and further unravel the molecular complexity of disease. This convergence of next-generation sequencing, AI and machine learning technologies and high-

performance computing provides a differentiated platform for developing the latest generation of advanced precision medicine diagnostic solutions for early detection, diagnosis, monitoring, therapy selection and drug development.

Caris was founded with a vision to realize the potential of precision medicine to improve the human condition. Headquartered in Irving, Texas, Caris has offices in Phoenix, New York, Cambridge (MA), Tokyo, Japan and Basel, Switzerland. Caris or its distributor partners provide services in the U.S. and other international markets.

More than half say the state's business climate has gotten worse, yet manufacturers expect gains in revenue, profitability, and capital investment.

"In addition to the consistent, historic headwinds they've had in the past â access to labor, the tax situation in Minnesota, some of the legislative mandates around family and medical leave â now you also have market-level uncertainty coming out of the Gulf that is affecting material prices. #5487. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5486. What we learned about the hyperscalers from earnings season

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Recently Amazon.com Inc., Google owner Alphabet Inc. and Microsoft Corp. reported earnings within roughly 24 hours of each other, and this earnings season told us more about long-term artificial intelligence strategy than any keynote or press release this year. Beneath the headlines lie three very different strategies.

Here’s what I took away: Amazon will be the long-term winner because its open, platform-first approach gives customers the broadest choice of models and silicon, and it’s showing that size doesn’t limit scale. Microsoft is a solid second, protected less by strategy than by the customers it already has locked in. And Google will be a distant third, with impressive technology built on a fragile business foundation and a closed, Gemini-first strategy that runs counter to where enterprises are heading.

The most remarkable part of the earnings season was that Amazon’s Amazon Web Services business has found a way to buck the law of large numbers. It’s growing 39.3% at its size. AWS revenue reached $46 billion, marking its sixth straight quarter of acceleration and its fastest growth in nearly five years, putting the business at an $184 billion annualized run rate, according to Amazon’s third-quarter release.

To put that in perspective, the last time AWS grew this fast was in the fourth quarter of 2021, when it posted 40% growth on $17.8 billion in quarterly revenue. AWS is now more than two-and-a-half times that size and is growing at essentially the same rate. The roughly $13 billion it added year over year is about three-quarters of what the entire business generated in a quarter back then.

The law of large numbers is supposed to catch every business. The largest cloud provider on the planet is accelerating instead.

Amazon Chief Executive Andy Jassy projected AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Operating income reached $17.8 billion at a 38.7% margin, and backlog climbed to $578 billion, up from $244 billion at the end of 2025. On the earnings call, Jassy indicated AWS could reach $1 trillion in as little as five years, giving Amazon two businesses that do north of a trillion dollars in revenue.

Bedrock is the most underappreciated piece of Amazon’s strategy and, in the long term, the most important. Microsoft built its AI identity around OpenAI, and Google around Gemini. Both host third-party models, but each has a house favorite that its roadmap and pricing orbit around. AWS made model neutrality the product.

According to an AWS Builder Center guide, Bedrock offers more than 100 models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Google, xAI and Nvidia. In the third quarter alone, Amazon added OpenAI’s GPT-6 family, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, xAI’s Grok 4.7, and Moonshot’s Kimi K3, per Amazon’s quarterly release.

The open-weight wave makes this even more important. Bedrock already runs DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Kimi, Gemma, Nemotron and OpenAI’s gpt-oss models as fully managed services, as AWS has detailed. As open models close the gap, enterprises will fine-tune smaller, cheaper models for specific tasks and reserve frontier models for the hardest problems. The platform that lets them route across all of them under a single security and governance model wins. A cloud built around a single-model company has a conflict of interest every time an open model gets good enough to replace it.

Customer spending is validating Bedrock’s value, as Fortune 500 spending on Bedrock rose nearly sevenfold year over year and token volume grew nearly 17-fold, Jassy said on the earnings call.

The second advantage is silicon, which is tightly linked to Bedrock. Most of Bedrock’s inference runs on Trainium, which lets AWS keep prices low while protecting margins, according to TIKR’s call coverage. Customers using Amazon’s custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in the third quarter alone, as noted in the call transcript.

The bigger news was Jassy’s commitment to sell Trainium outside AWS starting in late 2027. “We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” he said, according to Yahoo Finance. Training is periodic, whereas inference is a perpetual cost that scales with every agent and transaction. Selling Trainium racks brings AWS’ price-performance to enterprise data centers, sovereign environments and neoclouds, and gives organizations that need on-premises inference a credible alternative to Nvidia.

AWS has the broadest infrastructure footprint, the broadest model selection, and silicon that lowers the cost per token. The downside is the bill: a 2026 capex of roughly $220 billion, per 24/7 Wall St., and negative $33.5 billion in free cash flow, according to TradingKey. That spending is backed by contracted demand. If the growth rate continues, investors should be happy to see Amazon spending ahead of demand, but all eyes will be on free cash flow.

Who builds on AWS: Builders, including digital natives, AI labs, independent software vendors and large enterprises with mature engineering teams seeking model choice, cost control and no dependence on a single model partner.

Of the three hyperscalers, Microsoft’s business is the most predictable because it’s very hard to disrupt and isn’t a disruptor. What it is now is likely what it will be in the future. Azure grew 48% to $33.2 billion, the first time Microsoft has disclosed Azure revenue in dollars, according to CNBC.

But the most notable data point concerned lock-in. Customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats grew more than eightfold year over year, including Capgemini, Hitachi, Truist and the U.K.’s HMRC, according to Microsoft’s earnings call. That’s Microsoft’s true AI strategy: Upsell AI to the hundreds of millions of workers already living in Office, Teams and Windows. Switching costs are enormous, and Microsoft will capture a large share of enterprise AI spend regardless of how its models compare.

Google and others have tried to disrupt the Office franchise for decades but haven’t posed a serious threat. In the AI era, a company like Canva or Zoom could introduce an entirely new way to create documents and begin to erode that business, but until there is a material loss of share, that installed base seems safe.

Microsoft’s strategy has downsides. The company leans heavily on OpenAI, a partner that increasingly acts like a competitor. On the same earnings call, Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries were delayed. Microsoft also didn’t update its total paid Copilot seat count, leaving open how deeply those seats are used.

Who builds on Microsoft: Large, Microsoft-standardized enterprises, especially in regulated industries and the public sector, prioritize knowledge-worker productivity within the tools they already use.

Google Cloud’s headline numbers were impressive. Revenue grew 103% to $30.7 billion, and the operating margin was 36.2%, according to highlights from Alphabet’s earnings call. But a strong quarter doesn’t necessarily signal durability, and the earnings exposed three structural problems.

First, look at what is driving growth. According to Alphabet’s investor relations, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said tensor processing unit system sales were a “meaningful contributor” to cloud revenue. Hardware sales are lumpy and concentrated among a few large buyers, which is a different business from recurring cloud consumption.

Second, the core business funding all of this is showing cracks. Search made up 49.7% of Alphabet’s revenue, below half for the first time in the company’s history. That trend is likely to continue given the diversity of AI platforms. A year earlier, it was 55.3%. Also, Search grew only 12%, down from 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2. YouTube ad revenue grew 9.2% to $11.21 billion, short of analysts’ $11.43 billion expectation. That’s down 15% from a year earlier and 13% from last quarter, adding only $152 million over the last quarter.

Third, spending is outpacing cash. Capex reached $51.4 billion, while free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. Alphabet expects capex to exceed $300 billion in 2027, according to CNBC. The core business’s decline is becoming significant as the capex arms race continues.

Google has world-class research, Gemini and TPUs. Against that, it has a Gemini-first strategy that sits awkwardly with the open-weight wave, an ad business under AI pressure, and a history of sunsetting products, which remains the biggest objection I hear from chief information officers. Also, Google has always struggled with its enterprise strategy.

In 2018, I wrote this post for CIO.com asking whether Google was ever going to get serious about enterprise, and nothing much has changed. It seems to roll out products that have promise but never makes them best-in-class. As an example, Google Meet is good but not great, and Docs, Gmail and Drive are the same. They’re low-cost, but there are always better alternatives. Why would we expect their AI strategy to be different?

Who builds on Google: AI-native startups, research-heavy organizations,and BigQuery shops willing to accept platform risk. It’s a harder sell to a regulated enterprise making a 10-year commitment.

Neither is likely to make a long-term dent in the hyperscaler market, for one simple reason: They lack the flywheel. Amazon has retail and advertising; Google has search; and Microsoft has Office and Windows, each massive cash-generating businesses that can fund a multiyear compute buildout. The AI infrastructure race is capital-intensive, and IBM and Oracle are running it without that engine.

Oracle’s numbers look impressive on the surface, with cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% to $7.4 billion in its September quarter and RPO at $664 billion. The problem is how it’s financing that growth. Capex hit $28 billion in a single quarter, free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion, and debt has reached $125 billion, according to CNBC. After a $20 billion equity sale, it’s now selling another $10 billion in bonds, as Yahoo Finance reported.

Its database business can’t fund this buildout, so Oracle is relying on borrowed money and customer prepayments. That’s a fragile way to compete with companies that can self-fund.

IBM has largely stayed out of the compute race. Revenue grew 5% to $17.1 billion, led by Red Hat, according to IBM’s earnings release. IBM’s presentation reports $7.8 billion in year-to-date free cash flow, roughly what Amazon or Microsoft spends on capex in two weeks. IBM will matter as a hybrid-cloud integration layer, not a primary AI platform.

The biggest takeaway from earnings season is that the hyperscaler AI race now has a predictable order. Amazon is growing nearly 40% at an $184 billion run rate by doing what it has always done: building an open platform from silicon to agents, offering the broadest shelf of frontier and open-weight models, and preparing to take its inference silicon beyond its own data centers. Microsoft is a strong second, monetizing its existing customer base. Google is a distant third, betting that superior technology can outlast disruption to its core business while asking customers to adopt a closed stack.

To be clear, when I say “distant third,” that’s a forward-looking statement. Currently, Google’s cloud business is only slightly smaller than Azure’s, so my basis for “distant third” is openness, customer trust, enterprise go-to-market and the ability to fund the buildout.

When AI becomes a line item in IT budgets, customers will gravitate toward the platform with the lowest inference costs, the broadest selection of models and the deepest operational track record. Openness wins platform wars.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5485. TheHolyCoins Launches Crypto Presale ROI Dashboard to Track Token Performance, Revealing 99.34% Average Loss

The crypto presale ROI tracker gives investors one place to compare token prices, track returns and assess the risks of new token sales.

TEL AVIV, Israel, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TheHolyCoins (https://theholycoins.com) has launched a crypto presale ROI dashboard tracking 48 projects, with an initial dataset showing a fundraising-weighted average decline of 99.34% from final presale prices. The dashboard helps investors examine what happened to tokens after previous sales before committing money to new ones. TheHolyCoins plans to expand coverage beyond the initial 48 projects.

The crypto presale performance tracker lets users compare final presale prices with current market prices, alongside reported funds raised, all-time highs and listing dates. Investors can search individual projects, filter by category and sort the results to see which tokens have retained value and which have collapsed.

BlockDAG and Pepe Unchained illustrate the scale. The tracker records $440 million in reported fundraising for BlockDAG and $73.9 million for Pepe Unchained. As of November 10, their tokens show returns of â99.96% and â99.82%, respectively, against the final presale prices used by the dashboard.

Those two projects alone account for more than half a billion dollars in reported fundraising. Their performance gives investors researching new crypto presales a reason to look beyond fundraising milestones and projected listing prices.

The list includes apparent scams alongside stalled projects. Bitcoin Pepe's team disappeared amid complaints of undelivered tokens, while Qubetics halted core development after reporting over $18 million raised. Others, including Pepe Unchained, continue developing products despite steep price declines and exchange delistings.

"Retail investors can face experienced developers and professional marketers who know how to sell the promise of getting in early," said Shay Feldman, editor-in-chief of TheHolyCoins. "Influencer endorsements, countdowns and ambitious price predictions can make a speculative token sale look like an opportunity investors cannot afford to miss. We built this dashboard so people can check what happened after previous presales ended, before putting their money into another one."

Coverage focuses on presales conducted from 2021 onward, primarily those raising approximately $1 million or more, with selected smaller projects included. Prices are sourced mainly from CoinGecko, while fundraising information comes from public materials and reporting.

Returns compare market prices with final presale prices; individual investor outcomes depend on entry prices and selling decisions. Calculations exclude vesting schedules, liquidity depth and OTC transactions. The dataset covers selected projects, rather than the entire crypto presale market.

#5484. Lupus Research Alliance Awards Lupus Insight Prize for Critical Discovery of TLR7 Immune Control Sensor Failure Driving Lupus

Prize Bestowed to Gregory Barton, PhD, University of California, Berkeley, and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and Olivia Majer, PhD, Cincinnati Children's

NEW YORK, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Lupus Research Alliance, the world's largest private funder of lupus research, proudly awarded the 2026 Lupus Insight Prize to Gregory Barton, PhD, University of California, Berkeley, and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and Olivia Majer, PhD, Cincinnati Children's, during ACR Convergence 2026 (November 6-11, Orlando), the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology. The Prize recognizes Drs. Barton and Majer's defining work revealing how UNC93B1, a key regulator of the immune system's RNAâsensing receptor TLR7, normally keeps immune responses in check and how genetic changes in this pathway can lead to disease, pointing to new opportunities for targeted treatments.

The Lupus Insight Prize is a signature honor of the Lupus Research Alliance, now in its 14th year, that awards $100,000 for a recent, seminal lupus discovery that shifts understanding or treatment of the disease. Co-recipients Dr. Barton and Dr. Majer were awarded the Prize during the ACR Convergence 2026 during the newly established Lupus Research Alliance Lupus Insight Prize Lectureship.

During a session moderated by Gary Koretzky, MD, PhD, Cornell University, Drs. Barton and Majer presented their seminal findings to an esteemed audience of clinicians, researchers, and members of the scientific community.

"The Lupus Insight Prize recognizes discoveries that have the power to transform how we understand and treat this complex disease," said Teodora Staeva, PhD, Chief Scientific Officer at the Lupus Research Alliance. "The work of Drs. Barton and Majer provides compelling insight into how the immune system loses its ability to distinguish self from non-self in lupus and helps identify patients who may benefit from therapies targeting the TLR7 pathway."

Uncovering the Missing Link Between TLR7 Dysregulation and Lupus

TLR7 is an immune sensor that helps the body detect viral infections by recognizing genetic material (RNA) from viruses. Because similar genetic material is present in the body's own cells, TLR7 must be tightly controlled to prevent it from mistakenly targeting healthy tissue. This control is partly managed by UNC93B1, a protein that directs where TLR7 travels inside cells and helps regulate when and where it can signal. Although abnormal TLR7 activity is recognized as a major driver of lupus, exactly how UNC93B1 restrains this pathway â and how its disruption leads to disease â had previously remained unclear.

In a landmark 2024 study, Dr. Barton and his team, which included Dr. Majer during her postdoctoral training, performed the first systematic analysis of UNC93B1 â testing the effects of more than 100 genetic mutations across the protein. The team identified dozens of variants that increase TLR7 activity â far more than expected â and showed that several of these same mutations are present in individuals with lupus. Importantly, mice engineered to carry these mutations developed severe lupus-like disease, showing that disruption of UNC93B1 can directly drive autoimmunity.

"We were surprised by how many mutations in UNC93B1 could amplify TLR7 activity," said Dr. Barton, whose work has been previously funded by several Lupus Research Alliance grants. "Our findings reveal just how precisely this pathway must be controlledâ and how even small changes can push the immune system toward disease."

Building on these findings in her own lab, Dr. Majer uncovered how a disease-causing UNC93B1 mutation works at a molecular level in a child with early-onset lupus. Her findings revealed that UNC93B1 normally partners with a cellular complex called BORC to help ensure that activated TLR7 is properly degraded once its job is done. The lupus-associated mutation disrupts this process, allowing TLR7 to accumulate inside immune cells and become overly responsive to the body's own RNA.

Together, these studies establish UNC93B1 as a critical safeguard that keeps TLR7 activity in check. Dr. Barton's work maps the landscape of UNC93B1 mutations that can drive excessive immune activation, while Dr. Majer's studies explain how defects in this pathway lead to disease at the molecular level. Collectively, their findings deepen understanding of how immune balance is maintained and provide a foundation for more precise approaches to diagnosing and treating lupus by restoring proper TLR7 regulation.

"Understanding this pathway and its role in lupus development will help provide patients with a more definitive diagnosis and identify better opportunities for therapeutic intervention," Dr. Majer said. "If we can identify patients with these specific mutations, we can begin to match them with therapies that more directly target the underlying cause."

Dr. Barton is Co-Chair of the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator, and C.H. Li Distinguished Professor of Immunology and Molecular Medicine. Dr. Majer is an Associate Professor of Immunology in the University of Cincinnati Department of Pediatrics and leads an Immunobiology lab at Cincinnati Children's. She previously conducted postdoctoral research in Dr. Barton's laboratory at UC Berkeley.

To learn more about the Lupus Insight Prize and past honorees, visit here.

About Lupus Lupus is a chronic, complex autoimmune disease that affects millions of people worldwide. In lupus, the immune system, meant to defend against infections, produces autoantibodies that mistake the body's own cells as foreign, causing other immune cells to attack organs such as the kidneys, brain, heart, lungs, and skin, as well as blood and joints. Ninety percent of people with lupus are women, most often diagnosed between the ages of 15-45. Black, Latinx, Indigenous, Asian and Pacific Islander people are disproportionately affected by lupus.

About the Lupus Research AllianceThe Lupus Research Alliance is the largest non-governmental, non-profit funder of lupus research worldwide. The organization aims to transform treatment by funding the most innovative lupus research, fostering scientific talent, and driving discovery toward better diagnostics, improved treatments and, ultimately, a cure for lupus. Because the Lupus Research Alliance's Board of Directors funds all administrative and fundraising costs, 100% of all donations go to support lupus research programs.

For more information or to donate to lupus research, visit the LRA at LupusResearch.org and on social media at: X, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram.

#5483. Hanbat National University Researchers Find Way to Improve OLED Efficiency and Lifespan

Researchers tune a thin internal layer to reduce charge-related light loss and extend OLED device lifetime.

CHUNGCHEONG PROVINCE, South Korea, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) power many display screens, but their efficiency can be limited by energy lost inside the device. As organic layers are deposited, their molecules can align to create an internal electrical potential known as giant surface potential (GSP). When this potential draws excess positive charges, or holes, near the light-emitting layer, they can interfere with light-producing excitons. This process, called excitonâpolaron quenching, reduces emitted light and can affect device performance.

A research team was led by Professor Jae-Hyun Lee from the Department of Creative Convergence Engineering at Hanbat National University, Republic of Korea, along with Dr. Jong Soo Kim from the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology. The researchers placed thin electron-blocking layers (EBLs) between the hole-transport and light-emitting layers to adjust the local electrical environment. They compared materials with negative GSP values of â1, â40 and â87 millivolts per nanometer, using electrical measurements, impedance spectroscopy, transient electroluminescence, and photoluminescence to examine charge movement and light loss. This paper was made available online on July 7, 2026, and was published in Volume 545 of the Chemical Engineering Journal on October 1, 2026.

The measurements showed that negative GSP could counter the emitting layer's positive potential and regulate unwanted hole injection. Impedance and transient electroluminescence data revealed that the stronger the negative GSP, the more holes were held at the interface with the emitting layer. The o-CBP layer, with a GSP of â40 millivolts per nanometer, provided the best balance in the tested devices. "The key is to control the interface potential between layers, rather than simply using a material with the strongest GSP," said Prof. Lee.

The strongest negative GSP was not the best option. PhCzCz-PhTPS, at â87 millivolts per nanometer, trapped holes strongly at the interface and also restricted charge injection too much. This reduced current and the likelihood of forming light-emitting excitons, lowering efficiency and shortening device lifetime. By contrast, the o-CBP device reached an LT95 lifetime of 35 hours, compared with about 29 hours for the reference, approximately 20% longer. LT95 measures the time for luminance to fall to 95% of its initial level under the study's test conditions. "Our results show that an intermediate negative surface potential can reduce energy loss while preserving the charge flow needed for light emission," said Prof. Lee.

The findings suggest a design strategy for OLED technology: treat interfacial electrostatics as an adjustable property, not simply a consequence of the materials. Better control of charge accumulation could support energy-efficient displays and longer-lasting screens in smartphones, televisions, monitors and emerging foldable or wearable devices. However, these experiments tested OLEDs under laboratory conditions; they do not establish longer battery life, reduced burn-in, or improved image quality in commercial products.

Overall, the study shows that negative GSP should be tuned to the surrounding layers, not maximized. This principle may also inform other organic electronics where interfacial charge accumulation contributes to energy loss. Further testing across device designs and operating conditions is needed to determine how broadly the approach can improve real-world display performance.

Title of original paper: Negative giant surface potential engineering for suppressing excitonâpolaron quenching in organic light-emitting diodes

Journal: Chemical Engineering Journal DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2026.179183

#5481. Industrial automation startup Path Robotics raises $300M in funding

Path Robotics Inc., a startup working to automate industrial welding workflows, today announced that it has raised $300 million in funding.

Georgian led the Series E round. It was joined by a consortium that included the venture capital arms of Yamaha Motor Co. and Navier Corp., one of South Korea’s largest tech firms. The investment gives Path Robotics a post-money valuation of $2.45 billion.

Welding tasks were historically difficult to automate because of a phenomenon called heat-induced metal distortion. It occurs when the heat produced by a welding torch warps the metal parts being joined together. Furthermore, the parts change shape again when they cool down. Those distortions are often unpredictable, which means they can throw off a robot arm that follows a static, pre-programmed welding plan.

There are also other sources of complexity. Mass produced metal parts that are based on the same blueprint often differ slightly because of manufacturing inconsistencies. In many cases, those variations make it necessary to adjust the way welding is performed. That isn’t always possible with traditional automation software.

Path Robotics has developed an AI model that addresses those challenges. Obsidian, as it’s called, is specifically designed to power industrial robots equipped with welding torches. The company says that the model can observe how metal parts change shape during the welding process and adjust its workflow accordingly. Furthermore, it automatically accounts for unexpected part variations.

Obsidian monitors the welding workflow using four lasers attached to the torch that it controls. The emitters illuminate the parts being welded together and the reflected light is captured by a pair of cameras. According to Path Robotics, Obsidian collects data not only during the welding process but also before and after each run.

The data powers an AI model that the company refers to as a weld world model. Path Robotics’ researchers use it to generate simulated welding projects. Those simulations, in turn, power Obsidian’s training workflow.

Path Robotics originally developed Obsidian for large robotic workstations called welding cells. In April, it introduced a four-legged robot called Rove that uses the model to automate shipbuilding tasks. The company says its software can also be used to make parts for vehicles, power generators, utility poles and other heavy equipment.

“We’re seeing accelerating demand from manufacturers that need to expand production capacity but can’t get there with traditional automation,” said Path Robotics co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Andy Lonsberry. “This capital allows us to scale our welding business alongside our customers while investing further in the data, compute, and model development needed to take on every task before and after welding.”

#5480. CoreWeave stock jumps 11% as earnings beat eases AI slowdown fears

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The AI cloud provider lifted its full-year revenue guidance to $13.0 billion-$13.3 billion and reported a $132.5 billion backlog

CoreWeave raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion after it reported third-quarter results on Tuesday that included revenue of $3.66 billion.

CoreWeave stock was up 11% before the opening bell on Wednesday. Shares of Nebius, Applied Digital and IREN rose in premarket trading as well.

Third-quarter revenue compared with $1.365 billion a year earlier. The company lost $709 million, or $1.27 per share, compared with a $110 million loss, or 22 cents per share, in the third quarter of 2025.

Adjusted loss was 95 cents a share, according to CNBC. Analysts had expected a loss of $1.16 a share and revenue of $3.55 billion.

CoreWeave raised its full-year adjusted operating income guidance to a range of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, a 26% increase at the midpoint from prior guidance. Analysts had forecast adjusted operating income of $1.07 billion and 2026 revenue of $12.86 billion, according to CNBC. The company's August revenue guidance was $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion.

The company now expects capital expenditures of $37 billion to $39 billion for the year, up from a prior range of $35 billion to $39 billion. It cited an expectation of delivering infrastructure to customers on an earlier schedule than planned. It continues to expect more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power at year-end and raised its annualized run-rate revenue guidance to $20 billion to $21 billion to exit 2026.

Revenue backlog was about $132.5 billion as of Sept. 30. That compares with $104 billion at the end of June.

"Our growth is supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contracts, operating cash flow, and approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone," CEO Michael Intrator said in a statement.

CoreWeave stock is down more than 40% from where it traded a month ago. Investors had questioned the company's heavy borrowing amid rising interest rates, according to Reuters.

Chief Financial Officer Nitin Agrawal said during the earnings call that CoreWeave has no plans to sell more unsecured bonds at the parent-company level through 2027 while yields remain where they are, according to CNBC. He projected that CoreWeave will raise less than $5 billion in debt at the parent level through 2027.

According to Reuters, CoreWeave expects its adjusted results to turn profitable during the opening six months of 2028.
