#5479. Famous Investors Face a Nov. 16 Holdings Deadline While Recent Filings Fill In the Gap

NEW YORK, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Market Updates News Commentary - Investors who follow Warren Buffett, Bill Ackman and Michael Burry by the paperwork they leave behind have a date circled. Under the Securities and Exchange Commission's published schedule, Form 13F holdings reports for the quarter that ended Sept. 30, 2026 are due Monday, Nov. 16. Until those arrive, the latest 13F reports on file from the firms tied to two of them cover June 30, the filing history of the third stops in late 2025, and companies connected to those filings have reported results over the past two weeks. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (NYSE: BRK.B), Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL), Sirius XM Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: SIRI), Howard Hughes Holdings Inc. (NYSE: HHH), and Restaurant Brands International Inc. (NYSE: QSR).

According to the SEC staff's frequently asked questions about Form 13F, each report is due within 45 days after the end of a calendar quarter, and when that deadline falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the first business day after. The 45th day after Sept. 30 is Saturday, Nov. 14, and the SEC lists Monday, Nov. 16, 2026 as the deadline for the third quarter of 2026.

The same guidance says a 13F lists the issuer, the class of security, the number of shares owned and their fair market value as of the end of the calendar quarter, and that short positions are not included. That means the reports due next week will describe holdings as of Sept. 30, not what any manager owns on the day a report is posted.

Berkshire reports under a new leadership lineup

Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (NYSE: BRK.B) published its third quarter 2026 results on Nov. 7 and filed its 10-Q on Nov. 9. Operating earnings were $12,705 million, compared with $13,485 million a year earlier, and the company said it acquired approximately $9.6 billion in treasury shares during the quarter, bringing the nine-month total to about $14.4 billion. Insurance float was approximately $178.5 billion at Sept. 30.

The 10-Q's certification was signed by Gregory E. Abel as President and Principal Executive Officer, and a Sept. 18 release on Berkshire's website is titled "Warren E. Buffett Becomes Chairman Emeritus, Remains Director; Howard G. Buffett Elected Chairman." The 10-Q shows purchases of equity securities of $41,771 million and sales of $30,572 million in the first nine months of 2026, along with $336.7 billion of short-term investments in U.S. Treasury Bills on the Insurance and Other balance sheet at Sept. 30.

Two Berkshire holdings with fresh numbers

Berkshire's 10-Q names Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) among its five largest holdings at Sept. 30, 2026, and Berkshire's 13F for June 30 lists 227,917,808 Apple shares, the same count as in its March 31 report. Apple's fiscal fourth quarter results, released Nov. 2 for the quarter ended Sept. 26, showed revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year over year, and diluted earnings per share of $2.10, up 14 percent, including a favorable impact of $0.05 from tariff refunds.

Apple's release cited all-time record revenue of $479 billion for fiscal 2026 and $28 billion returned to shareholders during the quarter. Apple's board of directors also declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share, payable on Nov. 16, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on Nov. 12, 2026.

The same June 30 report lists 124,807,117 shares of Sirius XM Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: SIRI), unchanged from March 31. In its third quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29, the company reported revenue of $2.15 billion, down slightly year over year, which it said primarily reflected lower equipment revenue due to higher memory costs. Net income increased 7% to $317 million and free cash flow increased 14% to $293 million.

SiriusXM raised its full year 2026 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, lifting each of its three key financial metrics by $25 million, to approximately $8.55 billion in revenue, approximately $2.65 billion in adjusted EBITDA and approximately $1.40 billion in free cash flow.

Ackman's filings point to two operating companies

Bill Ackman is CEO of Pershing Square Inc., according to its Nov. 2 third quarter release, which describes Pershing Square Capital Management, L.P. as a wholly owned subsidiary. For June 30, 2026, Pershing Square Capital Management filed a 13F notice stating that its holdings are now included in the report of its public parent company, Pershing Square Inc. That report, filed Aug. 14, is the most recent 13F on file for Pershing Square Inc.

It lists two entries in Howard Hughes Holdings Inc. (NYSE: HHH) common stock totaling 27,852,064 shares. Howard Hughes' 10-Q describes Pershing Square as a related party because of its ownership interest and its representation on the board, and says that on June 4 it entered into a subscription agreement under which it issued and sold 140,000 shares of Series A preferred stock to an affiliate of Pershing Square for $1.0 billion. In third quarter 2026 results released Nov. 5, Howard Hughes reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $1.1 million, compared with net income of $119.5 million a year earlier.

The company said Total Operating Assets NOI, including contributions from unconsolidated ventures, increased 8% to $73.0 million, and it announced an intention to transition its real estate model to an asset-light real estate development and asset management platform by monetizing select real estate assets through asset sales and joint ventures.

The same Pershing Square report lists 25,821,284 shares of Restaurant Brands International Inc. (NYSE: QSR), which owns the Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes and Firehouse Subs brands. In its third quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29, the company reported consolidated system-wide sales growth of 6.2%, including 9.0% in International, and global comparable sales of 3.8%, including 8.4% at BK US.

Diluted earnings per share from continuing operations were $1.54, compared with $0.96 a year earlier, and adjusted diluted earnings per share were $1.10, compared with $1.03. The company said it has returned $1.3 billion of capital to shareholders year to date through dividends and share repurchases and remains on track for 8% organic adjusted operating income growth in 2026.

Scion Asset Management, LLC, whose most recent 13F was signed by Michael J. Burry as Chief Executive Officer, is a different case. Its EDGAR filing index lists a Form 13F filed Nov. 3, 2025 for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025 as its most recent filing, and no later filing appears on the index as of Nov. 10, 2026. That report reflects positions as of Sept. 30, 2025, so it does not describe holdings at any date in 2026.

#5478. Open Frontier Launches The First Rung Initiative to Keep the AI Economy Open to Young Workers, Founders and Small Businesses

New white paper and three-state polling call for AI safeguards paired with practical pathways into work, entrepreneurship and economic opportunity

WASHINGTON, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As artificial intelligence reshapes the workplace and the economy, Open Frontier this week released The First Rung Initiative, a new white paper outlining a policy agenda to ensure young Americans, workers in transition and small businesses are not left behind by the opportunities created by AI. Open Frontier Executive Director Erik Balsbaugh discussed the paper's key findings with journalist Aaron Parnas on Nov. 10.

The white paper is informed by new polling in Michigan, Nevada and South Carolina, which finds that while Americans are already using AI, many remain unconvinced that its benefits will reach ordinary people. Seventy-three percent of voters surveyed said they used an AI tool in the past year, but only twenty-nine percent expect AI to create jobs in their local community. Seventy-seven percent said they have little or no trust that the government will ensure AI benefits ordinary people.

"Early opportunities for young people cannot disappear as AI changes how Americans work. This is about pairing responsible guardrails with real access to the opportunities AI can create," said Erik Balsbaugh, Executive Director of Open Frontier.

The First Rung Initiative proposes a federal framework that pairs meaningful AI safeguards with practical measures to broaden economic access, including:

The paper draws on successful models that expanded opportunity at scale, including the GI Bill, rural electrification and Year Up. It also recommends a 12-month pilot program in South Carolina, Nevada, Michigan and one professional-services metro to test approaches that can be scaled nationally.

#5477. U.K. regulator warned McCormick-Unilever food deal may hurt competition

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Competition and Markets Authority gave the companies until Nov. 18 to offer remedies or face an in-depth review

The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority cautioned on Wednesday that McCormick's planned merger with Unilever's food business may reduce competition in at least one British market, according to The Wall Street Journal. The combined company would carry a value above $65 billion once debt is counted.

McCormick and Unilever must put forward commitments that resolve the concerns by Nov. 18, or the case moves to a more extensive phase 2 investigation, according to Bloomberg. An in-depth review has three possible outcomes: unconditional approval, approval conditioned on fixes such as asset sales, or a prohibition of the deal, according to RTÉ.

The CMA’s concerns center on two product categories sold to U.K. retailers: dry ingredient mixes, including chili con carne mixes, and dry sauces like parsley sauce, according to RTÉ. McCormick owns Schwartz, while Unilever’s food arm counts Knorr and Colman’s among its labels, so the merger would unite the largest two branded sellers of such goods, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The CMA views rivals such as Nestlé’s Maggi, Premier Foods’ Bisto and supermarket own-brands as limited competition, according to RTÉ. The regulator also said the merger would raise barriers for rivals trying to break into or grow within the two categories, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The CMA raised no concerns about mustard. It determined that English, French and American-style mustards each form their own market, since consumers don't treat them as near-interchangeable, according to RTÉ. As a result, the CMA concluded that McCormick's French's brand is not a close rival to either Colman's or Maille, both of which Unilever owns.

A Unilever spokesperson described the decision as an expected step and said the company is working with the CMA on a suitable remedy, according to RTÉ. Unilever said it had already resolved to divest Colman's, including the brand and its assets, to ease potential competition concerns, and that "discussions with potential buyers are progressing well," according to Bloomberg. McCormick also said it was working with the CMA, according to RTÉ.

Spokespeople for both companies said they remain confident of a timely closing, according to Bloomberg. The companies agreed to the deal in March and had signaled that they anticipated completing it around mid-2027, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Unilever stock was down 2.4% in early London trading on Wednesday.

#5476. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5474. BYD apologized for installing wheel rims backward on its Great Tang SUVs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The carmaker blamed a supplier error, said handling was not affected and restarted the warranty for affected owners

BYD apologized on Wednesday after a factory mix-up swapped the wheel rims between the front and back axles on certain Great Tang electric SUVs, according to Bloomberg.

BYD said in a Weibo statement that its investigation pinned the fault on a supplier based in Hubei, according to Bloomberg. The supplier, Hubei Boyu Industrial, made a code entry error that led to the wrong installation, according to CnEVPost.

BYD said it has corrected the faulty system, and the supplier has begun carrying out extra visual checks along its assembly line, according to Bloomberg. BYD's own testing found no effect on handling and no safety risk, the company said. It did not say how many vehicles were affected.

Owners with affected vehicles can have the rims replaced, and warranty coverage on their cars starts over as of Wednesday, according to Bloomberg. BYD will ask owners to bring their cars to nearby service centers, where the inspection and rim swap cost nothing, and it will supply replacement cars on loan or reimburse them for getting around, according to CnEVPost.

The mistake surfaced when a number of owners posted complaints on the internet, according to Bloomberg. They said the rear rims, which are the wider pair, were sitting on the front axle, while the narrower front pair had ended up on the rear axle. Some owners said they feared excessive tire wear and safety risks while driving.

The factory specification lists 8J×20 rims wrapped in 255/50R20 tires for the front axle and 9J×20 rims wrapped in 275/45R20 tires for the rear axle, according to owners cited by CnEVPost.

The Great Tang is the flagship of BYD’s Dynasty lineup and is priced from 239,900 yuan (about $35,800), according to Bloomberg. The model plays a key role in BYD’s move upmarket, and the company said it sold about 14,000 units in October.

No safety incidents were reported, according to Bloomberg. The error strikes a nerve for China's auto industry, where regulators are paying increasing attention to quality and durability.

#5473. Local Celebrities Terry Fox And Kenny Brooks Headline 6th Annual Neway Works Let's Shine Charity Gala At Ford House

November 13th fundraiser supports inner-city youth in metro Detroit

MOUNT CLEMENS, Mich., Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Michigan sports music artist Terry Fox, known as P.L., will emcee Neway Works' 6th Annual Let's Shine Gala on Friday, November 13, at the Edsel & Eleanor Ford House in Grosse Pointe Shores.

Fox is an Emmy-nominated sports music artist, rapper, and producer, known for Detroit Lions and Pistons game-day music. Detroit-born comedian and celebrity social media personality Kenny Brooks, known as "The Funny Salesman," with 2.1 million Instagram followers, will deliver the keynote.

Brooks, who grew up in Detroit facing financial hardship and began selling newspapers door to door around age 12, rose to massive fame on platforms like TikTok and Instagram by filming his unscripted, high-energy, and comedic door-to-door sales pitches. His personal testimony ties into Neway Works' mission to help inner-city youth across metro Detroit build on their strengths and explore career paths through mentoring and hands-on learning.

The annual Let's Shine Gala, themed "No Teen Without A Christmas," will raise funds that will be directed towards Christmas gifts, scholarships, and after-school youth enrichment programming for children, including sport and summer camps â helping young people in metro Detroit build brighter futures and achieve their full potential. Since its launch, the Let's Shine Gala has raised more than $200,000 for Neway Works. As the startup nonprofit grows, it aims to raise more through the gala to bring after-school youth development and mentoring resources to more young people across metro Detroit.

For Neway Works Founder Shane Gianino, the work goes back to his senior year at his alma matter Mount Clemens High School. He was diagnosed with cancer right before his breakout varsity basketball season but kept playing through chemotherapy. What sidelined him was academic ineligibility. Not chemotherapy. That experience as well as Shane's upbringing of being raised by his Grandparents and never meeting his dad, helped shape Project Transformation, the nonprofit's flagship after-school program.

"I wish someone had pulled me aside sooner and asked how I was doing in class during my senior year," said Gianino, Founder and Executive Director of Neway Works. "That's what makes this work so personal for me. I don't want any kid with a passion and dream to be benched because of grades."

The VIP cocktail reception begins at 6 p.m., general admission opens at 7 p.m., and seated plated dinner program begins at 7:30 p.m. at 1100 Lake Shore Road, Grosse Pointe Shores. Contact Neway Works for gala coverage or to discuss a follow-up visit to an after-school session.

About Neway Works. Founded in 2020 during COVID-19, Neway Works is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that helps young people succeed in school and develop life skills through after-school enrichment, tutoring and mentoring. Limited VIP tickets and Gala details are available at https://newayworks.org/lets-shine-gala/.

#5472. IBM Quantum announces upcoming Nighthawk r3 processor designed to execute 10,000 operations

IBM Corp. today announced the Quantum Nighthawk r3, its next-generation processor designed to tackle larger, more complex computations at high speed while maintaining quality.

The company also said that in 2027, IBM plans to link two r3 quantum processors into a single system capable of running up to 10,000 quantum operations, scaling to more than 1,000 qubits between them.

“Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental,” said Director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta. “IBM Nighthawk is already showing us what that looks like today.”

The new r3 chip follows the introduction of Nighthawk r2 in September, which supports more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 qubits.

Qubits are the fundamental unit of logical information in a quantum computer, similar to a classical computer’s bit. Unlike classical bits, which can be a 0 or 1, qubits can be 0, 1 or a “superposition” of both at the same time. Using this property, quantum processors such as IBM’s Nighthawk can do rapid, complex parallel calculations.

The r2 chip introduced a groundbreaking high-speed qubit reset architecture that lets developers and researchers quickly prime qubits after measurements. Under normal circumstances, after a quantum circuit runs and the result is measured, the qubits must return to the ground state before the next program can run; this process can take hundreds of milliseconds, meaning the chip remains idle during that time. With the new technology, this wait period can be reduced from about 200 milliseconds down to roughly 25 nanoseconds without disturbing neighboring qubits.

Building on lessons learned from Nighthawk r2 and the technology built into it, IBM said r3 will extend the same high-speed architecture to larger quantum systems to support 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits with 2,034 physical quantum components.

A physical qubit is the actual, hardware-level quantum device that stores the quantum information. In Nighthawk, the qubits are superconducting and arranged in a square lattice. The programmable qubits are the measurable, active quantum data units, while additional quantum components support them, including couplers and reset elements.

IBM said it has already demonstrated two critical technologies that will make combining two r3 chips. This year, the company connected two Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers, or “long-range” quantum interconnects. These act as a physical bridge between separate processors to create a larger machine.

In the demonstration, the couplers achieved a 99.4% transfer fidelity, progressing towards the target of 99.9% fidelity. The company also connected cryogenic modules into a single system.

In 2027, IBM intends to progress using these modularity advances to scale Nighthawk into a larger quantum system. By connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single 1,040 system, IBM will extend this high-performance architecture to tackle larger and more complex computations.

“As we scale this architecture to larger and more powerful quantum computers, the capabilities of quantum computation will reach new levels as we integrate more closely with classical resources and march ahead to fault tolerance,” added Gambetta.

IBM also announced that its cloud-based service for researchers and developers, IBM Quantum Platform, will bring high-performance classical and quantum computing together in a single managed environment.

Users can now integrate quantum workflows directly with HPC and classical resources on the platform, or with classical compute on their laptop or any number of the world’s most powerful supercomputers.

Integrating quantum and classical computing permits traditional computers to orchestrate algorithms and computations on specialized central processing units and graphics processing units, while the quantum computer runs parallel computations. Users are already seeing promising results, including Cleveland Clinic using the platform to process 2.6 million samples up to three times faster to model biological structures.

Direct integration of quantum and classical systems will also help drive breakthroughs in quantum error correction. Error correction is fundamental to handling the noise that can destabilize individual qubits, creating a high chance of errors rising out of computations. Quantum Platform is launching pulse-level access to give researchers precise control over how they can detect, understand and correct errors within quantum and classical architectures.

IBM recently launched a new quantum error-correction platform that addresses this, in collaboration with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The build physically colocates Nighthawk processors with next-generation AMD GPUs and CPUs.

#5471. OpenAI's quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion, but so did its losses

Free daily briefing on global business news.

OpenAI told investors its adjusted operating margin improved to -109% from -150% in the prior quarter, according to Bloomberg

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue in the three months ended in September, its first quarter at that level, according to Bloomberg. The ChatGPT maker’s operating loss for the period was $10.9 billion.

Revenue rose about 50% from the second quarter and was nearly three times the year-earlier level, according to Bloomberg. OpenAI shared the figures with investors on a call on Tuesday. President Greg Brockman and Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar spoke on the call.

OpenAI's adjusted operating margin stood at -109% in the third quarter, a smaller loss than the -150% recorded in the second quarter, according to Bloomberg. The company also informed investors that its annualized revenue stood at roughly $50 billion at the end of September. OpenAI declined to comment.

Bloomberg attributed the revenue increase to demand for OpenAI's latest AI software. It said OpenAI has won back traction thanks to newer models, lower prices and a push toward AI agents built to take over routine tasks for customers.

Rival Anthropic posted revenue of roughly $17 billion for the third quarter, according to Bloomberg. Its growth from the second quarter slowed to about 47%, versus a jump of over 140% in the prior quarter. The two companies have historically used different methods to arrive at their revenue numbers.

The latest figures follow a second quarter in which Anthropic surpassed OpenAI in quarterly revenue for the first time, with $11.6 billion against OpenAI's $6.7 billion. OpenAI's annualized revenue of about $50 billion in late September also fell short of a $68 billion figure that had been widely cited. That higher number included gross revenue from partner companies.

OpenAI is finalizing a fresh funding round that values it at $1.25 trillion, after pushing its public-listing timeline back to next year, according to Bloomberg. OpenAI recently closed an initial $11 billion part of that round. Anthropic is aiming to be valued at $1.4 trillion when it lists publicly later this month.

#5469. Anthropic is targeting up to $3.5 billion from Japanese investors in its IPO

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Japanese tranche is part of an IPO in which Anthropic is offering up to $64.4 billion of stock at about a $1 trillion valuation

Anthropic aims to draw between $3 billion and $3.5 billion from investors in Japan through its IPO, according to Bloomberg.

Anthropic plans to place 38.5 million to 50 million shares in Japan, with a preliminary price of $70 to $78 a share, according to a filing the company submitted to Japan's Ministry of Finance. Mizuho Securities will run the Japan portion of the sale, the filing said. Goldman Sachs $GS, Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley $MS Securities, Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities, Rakuten Group and SBI Holdings are among the firms responsible for taking orders from investors.

The Japanese portion is a public offering without listing, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg said Japan would be among the few markets where investors can buy directly into the IPO through this tranche, pointing to the country’s households and their ¥2.4 quadrillion (about $15 trillion) in financial assets.

The overall IPO covers up to $64.4 billion of Anthropic stock. Using the share count disclosed in a filing on Tuesday, that would put the company's worth at roughly $1 trillion, or about $1.4 trillion once all dilutive securities are included.

Anthropic is planning a Nasdaq $NDAQ debut under the ticker symbol “ANT,” according to CNBC. The company plans to price the offering on Nov. 18 and begin trading on Nov. 19. Anthropic is targeting about 20% of the offering for retail investors, compared with a typical 5% to 10% in IPOs, CNBC said.

Institutional demand is running ahead of SpaceX’s offering at the same stage, according to CNBC. Anthropic’s order book already holds enough demand to fill the deal between $70 and $78 a share, counting only allocable orders, CNBC said.

The $64.4 billion figure is the most Anthropic could raise, with any lower price meaning a smaller sum. Anthropic had been aiming for a valuation of $2 trillion up to a short time ago, according to CNBC. Some shareholders told CNBC they are no longer certain the company can reach even $1.5 trillion.

#5468. Your iPhone Duo Under Attack? Binance Flags Dangerous iOS Security Flaw

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance has warned Apple users about a dangerous iOS vulnerability that could expose crypto wallets, private keys, and login credentials. The flaw, called worse_query, allows malicious applications to access files normally isolated inside other apps. Binance warning identifies several affected iOS software versions and urges users to remove untrusted applications immediately.

The vulnerability threatens more than crypto wallets; apps storing sensitive information locally could also expose passwords, authentication data, and personal files. That makes the latest warning particularly concerning for iPhone users who rely on their devices for banking and crypto transactions.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

Binance says the problem affects iOS itself rather than its own wallet infrastructure. Users who suspect their devices have been compromised should create new wallets on clean devices and move their funds. The exchange also recommends resetting active login sessions and updating installed software.

The vulnerability exploits Apple’s application sandbox, a security mechanism designed to keep applications separated from one another. Normally, an application cannot freely access another application’s private files. This isolation protects sensitive information even when users install multiple applications on the same device.

This is where it gets dangerous: the worse_query exploit reportedly bypasses those restrictions. A malicious application could potentially access directories containing information belonging to other installed applications.

The researcher behind the public GitHub repository describes worse_query as a sandbox escape affecting iOS 26 and iOS 27. The project identifies affected releases spanning iOS 26.0 through 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2. Binance warns that exposed information could include cryptocurrency recovery phrases, private keys, and login credentials.

The actual danger depends partly on how individual applications store sensitive information. Wallets retaining recovery phrases or other credentials in accessible local files face particular risks.

Security researchers have also highlighted the importance of protecting plaintext wallet information. SlowMist’s security chief warned that the vulnerability could undermine assumptions about isolation between application containers.

Apple’s security update schedule adds another dimension to the Binance iOS warning. Apple’s security releases list iOS 27.2 and iOS 26.7.2 among its available software versions, both released on October 26, 2026.

However, Apple’s published security advisories do not explicitly identify worse_query by name. There is currently no confirmed public statement establishing that these updates fully resolve the specific sandbox escape.

A separate GitHub project implementing the exploit also reported on November 8 that Apple’s available software releases had not patched worse_query. This leaves users with an important gap between installing the latest available update and confirming that a particular vulnerability has been fixed.

Binance recommends installing the latest official iOS release and keeping all applications updated. It also urges users to remove applications from unknown sources, including manually signed IPA files.

For us, crypto holders, the safest response to suspected compromise goes beyond simply deleting suspicious software.

The latest iPhone warning follows several security incidents involving malicious applications and crypto credentials. In September, Binance warned users about FomoPeek, a third-party application whose versions 1.1 and 1.2 reportedly contained malicious code.

Security researchers found that the software could exploit iOS vulnerabilities to obtain elevated device privileges. Potentially exposed information included recovery phrases, private keys, login credentials, and other locally stored data.

More recently, CertiK highlighted the DarkSword exploit framework, which reportedly targeted cryptocurrency applications through compromised websites and vulnerable iPhones.

#CertiKInsight 🚨 A new version of DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit, is being used to target crypto wallets on unpatched iPhones. Simply opening a malicious site in Safari can be enough: no wallet connection, no signature needed. Here's what you need to know 🧵

These incidents involve separate attack methods. Nevertheless, they demonstrate why smartphone security has become increasingly important for crypto holders.

The Binance iOS warning highlights a fundamental problem with self-custody: protecting a recovery phrase means protecting every place where that information might be stored.

#5466. Nintendo's Zelda remake sold more than 5.2 million copies in its first four days

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Ocarina of Time remake posted the highest four-day sales of any Nintendo-published Switch 2 game, including 810,000 in Japan

Nintendo said “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” for Nintendo Switch 2 sold more than 5.2 million units in its first four days, including 810,000 units in Japan.

That is the highest global sales total for a Nintendo-published Switch 2 game in its first four days, the company said. The figure covers physical and digital versions.

The game launched Nov. 5 as a full remake of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time,” which came out for Nintendo 64 in 1998. Players control Link across two time periods, as Young Link and Adult Link, and use different abilities and items in each to advance. The remake has updated visuals and changes to playability while keeping the experience of the original, Nintendo said.

The game launched at $59.99 and sits at 96 out of 100 on Metacritic among both professional critics and players, according to Bloomberg.

Its four-day sales exceed the total sales to date of “Donkey Kong Bananza,” a 2025 release, according to Bloomberg. “Mario Kart World,” which shipped packaged with the Switch 2 console at its debut, is the only Switch 2 title that has outsold the remake.

The game also supports Zelda Notes, a service in the Nintendo Switch App for compatible smart devices, Nintendo said.

#5465. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5464. Nvidia stock rebounds premarket as Morgan Stanley cut it from top picks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia stock closed down 5.47% on Tuesday amid the scandal over CEO Jensen Huang's affair, with earnings due on Nov. 17

Nvidia $NVDA stock was up 5.3% in premarket trading on Wednesday as of 5:47 a.m. ET, bouncing back from two straight sessions of losses amid the scandal over CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.

Morgan Stanley $MS removed Nvidia from its list of top picks on Wednesday, according to CNBC. Nvidia stock had lost more than a quarter of its value since the bank first included it on Oct. 2. Analysts at the bank said in a note that Huang's leadership is "crucial" to where Nvidia is steering its strategy.

Nvidia stock ended Tuesday’s session 5.5% lower, with fresh reporting shedding light on the affair’s toll on the company.

Huang came back to work in person on Monday and sought to convey "business as usual," according to CNBC. He held meetings at the office on Tuesday, ahead of the company's earnings report on Nov. 17.

John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks, attributed the selloff to worries over possible new U.S. curbs and the chance that additional troubles could surface while the story unfolds, according to CNBC. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.

"It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, Nvidia retained law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the independent investigation its board announced Sunday. Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, will lead the work, and a panel of independent directors will supervise it. The board said on Sunday that nothing it has seen suggests Nvidia's trade secrets or U.S. national security were put at risk.

Huang apologized to employees in a message on Sunday. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote. The woman, Alice Huang, is not related to him and is suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of spying for China. China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the allegation unsubstantiated.

The Justice Department is conducting a criminal probe of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia AI chips to China. Rosen Law Firm has filed a shareholder class action against Nvidia and Huang in federal court in San Jose, California. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

#5462. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5460. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”

#5459. Nissan posted a net loss and cut its sales forecast as China slump deepens

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The automaker lowered its fiscal-year volume target to 2.97 million-3 million vehicles from 3.15 million, its second cut since August

Nissan Motor posted a net loss of ¥43.5 billion ($275 million) for the quarter ended Sept. 30 and cut its full-year global sales forecast as demand in China weakened.

Over the 12 months through March 2027, Nissan expects to sell 2.97 million to 3 million vehicles worldwide, a reduction from its earlier projection of 3.15 million. The company said China sales are under more strain than it had foreseen, pointing to soft demand, a quicker move toward new energy vehicles than predicted, and tougher competition.

The quarterly net loss narrowed from ¥106.2 billion a year earlier, a change the company tied to lower restructuring-related items. Net revenue rose 8.2% to ¥3.11 trillion. Operating profit fell to ¥2.1 billion from ¥51.5 billion, which Nissan attributed to the absence of last year's benefit from lower U.S. emissions-related expenses.

Analysts had expected operating profit of ¥54.9 billion, according to CNBC. They had also expected a net profit of ¥15.57 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Nissan kept its full-year operating profit forecast of ¥200 billion and its target of automotive net cash above ¥1 trillion at year-end. It expects ¥120 billion in operating profit in the second half. The company raised its sales outlook for the U.S. and Japan.

"China remains our most significant challenge, and we need to remain agile," CEO Ivan Espinosa said in a statement.

Espinosa told CNBC that Nissan intends to widen its lineup of China-developed vehicles for export, raising the count to five models from two and aiming at 12 regional market clusters in the "very near term." "We can defend ourselves from these very aggressive players by using exactly the same elements that they have: speed, cost, and good technology," he said.

Espinosa characterized China's market as a tough one in which volumes are falling steeply, according to The Wall Street Journal. Chief Financial Officer George Leondis said ending the year with a net profit is Nissan's top priority.

In August, Nissan trimmed its annual global sales target to 3.15 million vehicles from 3.3 million, citing persistent weakness in China. At the time, the company reported a net profit of ¥3.8 billion for the April-June quarter, its first quarterly profit in two years.

The company said its Re:Nissan restructuring plan generated ¥110 billion in additional cost savings in the first half. Nissan will announce a new business plan in February 2027.

#5458. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5457. U.S. mortgage rates fall to 7.21%, lifting home-purchase applications

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Mortgage Bankers Association's purchase index rose 7.5% for the week ended Nov. 6, while its refinance index gained 4.5%

In the week ended Nov. 6, the Mortgage Bankers Association said, the contract rate for a 30-year fixed loan dropped 9 basis points to 7.21%, according to Bloomberg. The decline was the fourth in a row, and the data came out Wednesday.

The group's index of home-purchase applications rose 7.5%, the largest weekly gain since mid-April, according to Bloomberg. It was the second time since the end of August that the weekly figure climbed.

The refinance index rose 4.5%, its third straight weekly gain, according to Bloomberg. The measure remains close to the weakest reading recorded since January 2025.

The latest reading follows a decline the week before. The 30-year rate had eased to 7.30% from 7.37% in the week ended Oct. 30, when purchase applications slid 2% from the prior week. That reading was the third straight weekly drop in the rate.

The rate had reached 7.50% in the week ended Oct. 9, the highest level since November 2023. Rates climbed back above 7% in mid-September, and the housing market has weakened since.

The National Association of Realtors said last month that pending home sales fell 7.3% in September from August. The index slid to 66.0, a record low for a data series that dates to 2001.

"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably," Yun said.

#5456. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5455. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5454. A venture capitalist warned Anthropic's IPO lockup could spark an AI correction

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Copper Sky's Jack Selby said a weak Anthropic offering and later lockup expirations could pressure the AI trade

Jack Selby, the head of the venture firm Copper Sky, warned that Anthropic's initial public offering could trigger a correction in the AI market, according to Bloomberg.

Selby, who also helps run Peter Thiel's family office as a managing partner, said the end of Anthropic's lockup periods could weigh on its stock. He named SoftBank Group and Oracle $ORCL as early warning signs, adding that Oracle is the more vulnerable of the two because it carries so much debt relative to its size.

"An underperforming Anthropic IPO has to be a very prominent player in what will be a pretty massive correction in the market with respect to AI," Selby told Bloomberg Television on Wednesday. "If the most anticipated AI company's IPO falls very short of its projected valuation, and just imagine where it's going to go after the lockups expire."

Anthropic hopes to bring in up to $100 billion from a private placement, the stock offering itself and any overallotment shares that may be sold, and early indications suggest demand is strong, according to Bloomberg. Selby is skeptical.

He said over 80% of what Anthropic earns does not repeat from period to period, which leaves it exposed whenever competitors get better. He pointed to DeepSeek and other Chinese models as another threat. "If they're six months or nine months behind what Anthropic does, what does Anthropic do that is so proprietary that it is better or has to be a national security interest versus these Chinese models?" Selby said.

Anthropic is targeting a valuation near $1.33 trillion, according to The Wall Street Journal, and the top of the range implies a fully diluted valuation as high as $1.405 trillion, according to CNBC. Investors had expected a valuation near $1.5 trillion before AI stocks sold off last Thursday, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Anthropic has agreed to sell $26 billion of Class N common stock in a private placement to Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom $AVGO, Google $GOOGL, Micron $MU, Microsoft $MSFT, Nvidia $NVDA and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Those shares are exempt from the underwriter lock-up agreements.

Torus raised $500 million in a Series C round to build a product about the size of a shipping container that pairs battery storage with AI computing power, according to Bloomberg. The Salt Lake City-based energy-storage startup said it will use the funding to build its Foundry product.

Magnetar led the round, with participation from ICONIQ Capital, Origin Ventures and Trinity Capital, according to Bloomberg. Hydra Host, a firm focused on AI infrastructure, counts itself as one of Torus’s customers, according to the startup.
