#5452. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5451. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5449. North Korea Hackers Launches Elon Musk Memecoins to Launder $6.4B Binance Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

North Korea backed hackers have created Elon Musk themed memecoins to launder stolen crypto in the $6.4 billion Binance hack. The hackers are using fake trading activity to disguise the movement of stolen funds.

One of the tokens featured Musk beneath an “Elon 2028 President” banner. Five others carried cartoon animals, crude jokes and familiar dog-coin branding. All six were created within three days and quickly abandoned.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic identified 117,000 NEAR tokens, worth $430,000, passing through the homemade coins between November 5 and November 7. The operation offers another look at how North Korea’s crypto laundering networks are adapting their techniques to move stolen assets.

Elliptic identified six newly created tokens on the NEAR blockchain: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI and SINU. Each token was paired with NEAR in its own decentralized exchange liquidity pool. The hackers then used one group of wallets to purchase the tokens with stolen NEAR before another group sold them back.

North Korea’s launderers are creating their own meme coins to move funds stolen from Binance.Between November 5 and 7, they launched at least six tokens on NEAR, dressed up with meme-coin logos such as a monkey in a pink bow and a duck in front of a US flag. Stolen NEAR went…

This separated the buying and selling wallets, preventing the stolen funds from moving directly between them. The transactions consequently resembled ordinary crypto trading, with the receiving wallets appearing to collect proceeds from successful memecoin trades.

Blockchain investigators could still follow the money. Elliptic found that almost all trading activity came from wallets connected to the laundering operation. Outside buyers accounted for less than 1% of one token’s trading volume.

The operation was also remarkably inexpensive. Creating each token cost just as low as 25 NEAR, or worth around $90. Five of the six token creators received funding from wallets that had already participated in earlier token sales.

The tokens were effectively disposable. All six stopped trading by November 8, with the creators of four withdrawing remaining liquidity.

The technique does not erase the transaction trail. Instead, it introduces additional steps that slow investigators trying to connect stolen funds with their eventual destinations. The firm previously identified a similar approach following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. North Korean launderers moved at least $24 million through homemade tokens using the same basic mechanism.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The memecoin operation represents only a small fraction of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance. The approximately $6.43 billion was taken from the exchange on October 29, making it the largest crypto theft ever recorded. Binance estimated its losses at $6.3 billion.

The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Investigators have identified multiple laundering techniques since the breach, including cryptocurrency swaps, cross-chain transfers, and movements through decentralized finance platforms.

Approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen, representing around 44% of the stolen assets. This leaves billions requiring further tracing as investigators race to identify wallets and freeze assets wherever possible.

🚨BINANCE HACK: $6.3B IMPACT, $3B FROZEN ON-CHAIN, LOSSES FULLY COVERED!Binance’s initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.No evidence of a wallet… pic.twitter.com/NA5taJLmv5

The use of North Korean hackers and memecoins adds another disposable layer to this operation. Rather than relying exclusively on conventional exchanges or direct wallet transfers, hackers can manufacture trading activity around virtually worthless tokens.

Meanwhile, Bitcoin’s expanding Layer 2 ecosystem is attracting developers looking to introduce faster transactions and programmable financial applications to the network.

Bitcoin Hyper is among the projects pursuing this approach, combining a Solana Virtual Machine-based execution environment with Bitcoin settlement. Its proposed infrastructure targets near-instant transaction finality alongside decentralized applications and DeFi functionality.

The project currently records more than $33.2 million raised in its presale, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136877 and staking rewards of 35% APY.

As crypto infrastructure continues to evolve, the race between increasingly sophisticated laundering networks and blockchain investigators is unlikely to slow down.

#5448. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5447. How Verizon’s CEO is rolling out his ‘play-to-win’ playbook—and fending off Elon Musk

Good morning. Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell writing this morning. Dan Schulman hates losing. For the past few years, he watched from his seat on Verizon’s board as the telecom giant lost market share, hobbled by internal bureaucracy and risk aversion.

“We were a big, lumbering giant that had fallen behind,” Schulman told me on the most recent episode of the Fortune 500 Titans and Disruptors podcast, admitting the board should have moved faster to make a leadership change. “We had processes where you needed something like 35 signatures before you could move forward.”

Schulman, who had been the board’s “hit-by-a-bus” successor, was named CEO in October 2025. At his first all-hands, he spoke candidly, without slides or notes: Verizon was losing. Layoffs were necessary. (Schulman would cut more than 13,000 roles, the largest layoff in Verizon’s history.) The culture had to be redefined. And the company’s tech stack needed to be rebuilt from top to bottom. (Schulman estimates there will be 100 billion AI agents in the next few years, driving an explosion in data traffic and network demand.)

“Culture is the single most important thing in any transformation. It is what holds you back or can propel you forward,” Schulman told me.

Schulman laid out a transformation plan he expects to take three years. He walked me through his playbook, including how he’s using AI to boost performance marketing and raise customer satisfaction, his views on AI-driven cybersecurity threats, and how he’s setting clear KPIs across 10 workstreams.

One year in, Verizon is beginning to see results, and it’s facing new challenges like Elon Musk’s Starlink.

Schulman says he hasn’t spoken with Musk recently. But he’s preparing for Musk to follow through and become a direct Verizon competitor.

“We’re not standing still. We’re assuming that what he says is what he’s going to do,” Schulman told me. “We need to be ready and prepared…We are going to have a radically different look and feel three or four years from now. We’re going to be two or three generations better than we are today.”

For Schulman’s full Verizon transformation playbook, listen to the episode of Fortune 500 Titans and Disruptors on Spotify. #5446. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5445. The Jay-Z leak was good news for the NFL. Its silence made it a problem

On Oct. 26, the NFL announced that Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl LXI halftime show at SoFi Stadium. That should have been a great story. He is a 25-time Grammy winner who sold out three Yankee Stadium shows this year.

It didn’t play out that way. The cause wasn’t the leak itself, but what came after. On Oct. 20, Puck reported that, according to multiple sources, Jay-Z had effectively “picked himself.” The report was not hostile. It described a consensus choice.

Then came the silence. For six days, the league and Roc Nation said nothing publicly. Into that gap came the Kaepernick storyline from the 2019 Roc Nation deal. Some viewed the deal as the NFL buying credibility and Jay-Z selling out.

When Commissioner Roger Goodell finally made the announcement, he said the right thing: “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that JAY-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him.”

That line could have run on Oct. 20 without spoiling a thing. It confirms nothing about the show, but frames the choice as the league’s own.

I’ve seen the opposite problem. In Beijing, the leak was hostile, and I had an hour.

I was handling PR for the NBA China Games on Oct. 10, 2012. Commissioner David Stern was due onstage for a press conference with the Chinese Basketball Association when a New York Times reporter called me.

I had been working with him on a good story that I pitched: the opening of a three-level NBA Center outside Beijing with basketball courts, an NBA store and an NBA cafe.

The reporter said the story would include the NBA Center but also focus on how the league had said it would build 12 NBA-style arenas in China and start an NBA China league. Neither happened, and he planned to explain how announcing the NBA Center was a step back from grander ambitions.

I alerted the head of our communications department and went to see then-Deputy Commissioner Adam Silver, who armed me with facts and rebuttals. Silver was calm and specific. That’s what an hour is for.

I went back to the reporter and walked him through our objections one by one. He pushed back on some and accepted others. The biggest win: I got him to hold the piece until after the press conference. It ran in print on Oct. 12.

We used that day well. Our department head and my teammates helped line up three positive features with other national outlets. I do not remember which outlets.

When the Times piece ran, it was better than we expected. The headline, “NBA Plans Complex Outside Beijing,” was mild. Our rebuttals shaped it, and the three features balanced what remained critical. Without that hour, the coverage out of Beijing could have been negative.

In Beijing, speed limited damage. At the NFL, speed would have preserved a good story. Friendly leaks cost more to ignore because no one feels the urgency.

The NFL may have been holding the news for its Monday Night Football slot. That’s a legitimate reason. But the league could have confirmed Goodell’s “one request” language without revealing the show.

I don’t know what the NFL was weighing internally. But when good news leaks, whoever speaks first sets the frame.

#5444. Fossil posted its first profit in years and raised its full-year outlook

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Fossil Group's third-quarter net income was $11.7 million, compared with a net loss of $39.9 million a year earlier

Fossil Group reported net income of $11.7 million for its fiscal third quarter and raised its full-year 2026 outlook, the company said on Tuesday. That compares with a net loss of $39.9 million a year earlier. Net income was $0.19 per diluted share.

Net sales rose 0.4% to $271.2 million, or 2.0% in constant currency. Operating income was $25.3 million, compared with an operating loss of $21.7 million in the prior-year period. Gross margin widened to 59.8% from 49.0%, which the company attributed to lower licensed brand minimum royalties, accelerated recognition of minimum royalties and better product margins in core categories. Operating expenses came in 11.1% lower, at $137.0 million.

Under its raised guidance, Fossil expects 2026 net sales of $980 million to $990 million and adjusted operating margin of 5.5% to 6.5%, both excluding currency effects. It also expects positive free cash flow. The prior outlook called for net sales to fall 3% to 5%.

"We are pleased that year-to-date results are outpacing our expectations, supporting an increase in our full year financial outlook on both the top and bottom line," CEO Franco Fogliato said in a statement.

In constant currency, net sales in Asia rose 15.1% and sales in the Americas rose 0.1%, while Europe fell 5.6%. Wholesale sales rose 4.4%, and direct-to-consumer sales fell 5.9%. Traditional watch sales rose 6.4%, while leathers fell 20.5% and jewelry fell 10.8%.

Fossil's store count fell to 174 from 204 over the year. The company said store rationalization reduced third-quarter sales by about 190 basis points.

Fogliato told CNBC that Fossil had not foreseen any increase in revenue for another 18 months. The company's previous quarterly net income dated back to the fiscal third quarter of 2022, according to CNBC.

#5443. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5442. Siemens Energy is targeting a 20% to 22% profit margin by 2030 after a record year

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The company proposed a €2.30 dividend and plans to buy back up to €9 billion more stock; its fiscal 2026 margin was 12.4%

Siemens Energy reported a record fiscal 2026 on Wednesday and set a target of a 20% to 22% profit margin before special items for fiscal 2030, the company said. It also aims to grow revenue by 12% to 14% a year through 2030.

Revenue grew 15.5% on a comparable basis to €44.2 billion ($49.5 billion) in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30. Profit before special items reached €5.5 billion, and the margin rose to 12.4% from 6.0% a year earlier. Net income was over €4.1 billion, compared with €1.7 billion in fiscal 2025. In the fourth quarter, net income was €1.36 billion, up from €236 million a year earlier.

Wind unit Siemens Gamesa reached break-even for the year, with profit before special items of €8 million, compared with a loss of €1.4 billion in fiscal 2025. Orders rose 18.8% on a comparable basis to €68.1 billion, and the order backlog reached a record €164 billion. Free cash flow before tax came in at €8.8 billion, above the company's target of around €8 billion.

"We delivered on our commitments: We met all raised guidance targets, significantly increased earnings and achieved break-even in our wind business," CEO Christian Bruch said in a statement. "Our 2030 targets set a clear direction and underline our level of ambition."

The company will propose a dividend of €2.30 per share for fiscal 2026, compared with €0.70 per share for fiscal 2025. It intends to devote as much as another €9 billion to buybacks of its own stock by the close of fiscal 2030. Shareholder returns for fiscal 2026, including buybacks, total €5 billion.

For fiscal 2027, Siemens Energy expects comparable revenue growth of 14% to 16% and a profit margin before special items of 14% to 16%. It forecasts net income of around €5 billion and free cash flow before tax of around €10 billion.

Siemens Energy stock rose 7.7% to €129 in European morning trade on Wednesday. Both the 2027 and 2030 guidance exceeded market expectations, according to The Wall Street Journal.

#5441. Brick houses are disappearing from America’s new construction: ‘Nobody got paid for how long a house would last’

Americans have never paid more for a home. The median existing home sold for a record $440,600 in June, according to the National Association of Realtors. Yet the brick house, the kind built to stand for a century, has nearly vanished from new construction.

Brick or brick veneer covered just 16.8% of new single-family homes started in 2025, down from almost a quarter in 2012, according to a National Association of Home Builders analysis of Census data. And most of the homes that still look like brick houses aren’t. They’re wood-frame houses with a layer of brick veneer attached to the outside.

A home can mean a lot of things. A place to raise a family. An investment. A refuge. A milestone. But somewhere along the way, American homebuilding changed the question. Not “will this last a lifetime?” Just “will it last the mortgage?”

“We didn’t decide to build houses that just outlast the mortgage. We kind of drifted there,” said Dan D’Agostino, founder of Plan Architecture and a residential architect based in New Jersey.

The distinction between real brick and veneer matters. A structural masonry wall holds up the building itself. Veneer is an exterior finish, while the wood frame behind it does the structural work.

The change reflects a postwar housing boom, a shrinking skilled-labor pool, rising construction costs, and a preference for homes that could be built quickly and cheaply. But some architects and builders say it also changed what Americans expect from the places they live, and what buyers paying record prices actually get for their money.

The shift away from structural masonry accelerated after World War II, when returning veterans and their families needed affordable homes, and needed them quickly. Developers such as Levitt & Sons met that demand with standardized designs and faster construction methods. Between 1947 and 1951, the company built 17,447 houses in Levittown on Long Island, at times finishing 10 to 12 homes a day.

“Levittown was a legitimate solution to a genuine crisis,” Steven Menotti, CEO of construction safety company Menotti Enterprise, told Fortune. “They needed shelter urgently, and a carpentry team got the job done faster than a masonry team ever would have.”

Brick construction requires skilled workers to lay individual bricks, one at a time. Wood framing can be assembled by crews with less specialized training, and it moves much faster. Matt DiBara, CEO of DiBara Masonry and a fourth-generation stonemason, said the economics were simple.

“It came down to cost and speed,” DiBara said. “After World War II the country needed homes that were more affordable and could be built in large batches, and a framing crew can close in a house way quicker and cheaper than a masonry crew can lay up solid walls.”

Brick veneer let builders keep the familiar look of masonry without relying on it to hold up the house. By the 1970s and 1980s, DiBara said, that approach had become standard.

The labor pool shrank along with it. Bricklaying is a specialized trade that takes years to master, while wood framing is easier to standardize and scale. The pressure hasn’t eased: the construction industry will need an estimated 456,000 new workers in 2027, according to the Associated Builders and Contractors.

“Today the hard part of building a true masonry house isn’t the brick. It’s finding people who can lay it,” D’Agostino said.

Jerel McCants, the architect overseeing the restoration of Tampa Union Station, which opened in 1912, sees the same problem. Skilled brick masons are not equally available across the country, he said, and regional differences in the workforce influence which materials builders choose. Brick’s beauty comes from the time and craftsmanship it demands.

“You can’t mass produce erecting a brick wall,” he told Fortune.

That distinction also complicates the historical record. Brick was the primary exterior wall material on 35% of new single-family homes completed in 1973, according to Census Bureau data. D’Agostino cautions against reading that as a measure of brick houses.

“That figure refers to brick veneer used as exterior cladding over wood frame construction. These are fundamentally different building systems,” he said.

Brick never disappeared entirely from American home exteriors. Its role as the structure holding a house up largely did.

The move to wood framing didn’t make every new home inferior. Modern construction offers advantages in insulation, building performance, and affordability, and amid an affordability crisis, the median price of a new home was $400,400 in September, according to the Census Bureau. New homes are now cheaper than existing ones for the first time in data going back to 1974, in part because builders are putting up smaller houses. But experts say homeowners lost some of what structural masonry provided.

Fire resistance is one. A masonry wall offers protection a decorative brick exterior cannot replicate.

“Whereas masonry walls will stand after a fire, the wood frame behind a veneer wall will burn just like any other wood frame if the fire gains access to it,” said Menotti, an FDNY-certified Construction Site Fire Safety Manager. “I see the results of this substitution frequently in my fire investigation work.”

D’Agostino points to another: the longevity of what’s hidden behind a home’s exterior.

“A real brick wall holds the house up, resists fire, evens out heat and cold, and with some repointing goes well past a hundred years,” he said. “Look at the old rowhouses in Philadelphia and Baltimore. With thin brick, the house only lasts as long as the wood and sheathing behind it, and those fail quietly.”

Not all veneer is equal, though. D’Agostino notes that full-depth brick veneer with an air gap behind it can serve as a durable rainscreen. His concern is with thinner brick products that lack those characteristics.

For McCants, the difference comes down to the materials themselves.

“Brick—it’s just dirt and water, right? So it’s going to be there forever,” he said. He estimates brick can last 100 years or longer, compared with roughly 30 years for some newer exterior products. Actual lifespans vary by material and installation, but he believes the industry has steadily traded permanence for convenience.

The shift also cost the trade its craft. Masonry demands specialized knowledge, from laying individual bricks to building arches, bonds, and decorative details.

“What I miss most is the craft. On an old brick building you can see the mason’s hand everywhere: the bond, the arches, the cornice, the way the joints were struck. Thin brick can copy the pattern, but there’s nobody’s hand in it. And once you stop building that way, you stop passing that knowledge down,” D’Agostino said.

Economics explains much of the shift. But architectural historian and geographer Thalia Toha, who studied at Princeton University and works at the Lafayette History Museum in Colorado, told Fortune that changing attitudes toward homeownership also played a role.

Brick’s place in American residential architecture has never been uniform, she said. In some communities, it was associated with urban commerce and traditional city buildings. The postwar suburban boom brought a new emphasis on affordability, customization, and distance from city life.

The American ideal of homeownership shifted, too.

“Before World War II, it was still fairly common for elders to live with adult children in a multi-generational agrarian setting. In the years following the servicemen’s return from the war, the American Dream narrative shifted. As a reward for their service, the grounding principle of homeownership is that every serviceman and their nuclear family deserves their own home. This includes a house separate from their older parents,” she said. “Because a house no longer necessarily had to last beyond one generation, brick’s timeless quality also loses value. One could also say that the one-generational time frame parallels with the single life of a 30-year mortgage time frame.”

McCants sees a similar change in how Americans live now. People relocate for jobs and other opportunities, he said, which has dulled the appeal of a home meant to stay in one family for a century.

“People don’t even stay in the same homes anymore like they used to, right? I grew up in the same house as a kid, you know, but nowadays people move every five to seven years into a new house,” he said.

The data is more mixed. The typical seller had owned their home for a record 11 years, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2025 buyer and seller profile, and buyers expect to stay 15. Still, few expect to hand a house down, and builders price accordingly.

“But that’s not the appeal to builders right now, because they want something that’s going to be quick, fast, and last just long enough for people to occupy,” McCants said.

D’Agostino sees the same tension between cost and longevity.

“The lower expectations for durability were a side effect. Once everything was built around speed, nobody got paid for how long a house would last,” he said.

Despite the economic and labor hurdles, some experts believe masonry could find a new foothold in American homebuilding.

Wildfires and other disasters have renewed interest in fire-resistant materials, particularly where homeowners face growing fire risk. DiBara also believes new construction technology could make brick more accessible by reducing the specialized labor it requires.

“We’re getting better at creating more modular systems for brick, like prefabricated brick veneer systems, and there are even brick kits with tools that set and level the mortar for a full brick,” DiBara said. “When it gets easier to lay brick and you don’t need five years plus to learn how, a lot more people can get into the trade and a lot more brick gets built.”

He sees demand for resilient construction as another catalyst.

“Look at the wildfires in California and all the natural disasters we keep seeing. People want something that holds up, and masonry is a much more resilient structure,” he said. “Put the demand for resilience together with systems that make brick easier to build, and I think brick makes a real comeback.”

Toha believes architectural revivals tend to follow broader cultural change. If car-dependent suburban development falls out of favor and homeowners gravitate toward urban-style architecture, brick could become more desirable again.

Not everyone expects structural masonry to return to the average American home. D’Agostino sees its future in specialized uses: fire-prone regions, historic urban neighborhoods, and buildings designed to last a century or longer.

“For the average house? I don’t think so. Back when everyone built with brick, it was the best technology around. Today we should use the best we’ve got, balancing performance and efficiency,” he said. “Doing it the old way just to be old-fashioned is fake, and it’ll never catch on.”

For McCants, the larger issue is whether the industry has any incentive to build homes that outlast their first owners.

“People move, people get jobs, people are very mobile nowadays. They move out of the city into different states,” he said. “It’s more of a transient lifestyle than what it was in the past, where people lived in the same place for generations. It’s not like that anymore.”

The homes going up today, if they last, will one day belong to someone who hasn’t been born yet. Whether they last is a decision builders are making now.

#5440. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5439. Tesla tuner Unplugged Performance is offering to take over the Cybertruck line

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The proposal would give Tesla a license fee and FSD revenue on each truck as it winds down production around mid-2027

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Unplugged Performance, an aftermarket tuner for Tesla $TSLA vehicles, offered on Tuesday to take over Cybertruck production from Tesla, according to Electrek. The company said a consortium of investors would fund the effort.

Unplugged Performance put its proposal to Tesla in a public post on X $TWTR, framing it as a standing invitation, according to Electrek. It said it would run Cybertruck production "at no cost to Tesla's floor space, headcount, or focus." Under the proposal, Tesla would receive a licensing fee on each vehicle built, as well as revenue from the FSD and Robotaxi networks.

The tuner said it backs making Tesla's Cybercab the top priority and would let that vehicle have priority access to battery cells. It said its lineup would consist of the Cybertruck, a CyberSUV with three rows of seats and a driverless CyberCargo hauler.

Unplugged Performance founder Ben Schaffer is comfortable with Tesla's pivot to self-driving technology but does not want the Cybertruck program to end, according to Electrek.

Investor Ross Gerber, co-founder of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth Management, quoted the post on X. "Free the tesla cybertruck," Gerber said, according to Benzinga.

Neither Elon Musk nor Tesla had responded to the offer when Electrek published its story on Tuesday.

The offer follows Musk's statement last week that Tesla would begin phasing out the Cybertruck at its Giga Texas plant around mid-2027, according to Electrek. Musk said Tesla needs to "make room for increased Cybercab production," according to Electrek.

Electrek reported that Cybertruck sales are at about 12% of Tesla's original target of 250,000 annual vehicles. Benzinga also reported that sales have fallen well below that target.

Unplugged Performance has a stake in the truck. It sells a range of Cybertruck products, among them lift and armor kits, and it has won multiple contracts to rebuild Cybertrucks as police cars for law enforcement, according to Electrek.

#5438. Inside Dan Schulman’s war on the old Verizon

The former PayPal CEO left a Montana ranch to shake up one of America’s most profitable companies.

At his first companywide meeting after becoming Verizon’s CEO in October 2025, Dan Schulman dispensed with the usual corporate pleasantries. Speaking without notes or slides, he delivered a message that employees of the telecommunications giant weren’t used to hearing from the top: Verizon had surrendered market share to AT&T, -T-Mobile, and lower-cost providers, and its sprawling bureaucracy had become a problem. The company was losing badly. And, he warned, layoffs were coming.

It was a stark introduction to a new leader who, until recently, had been watching the deterioration unfold from a seat on Verizon’s board. Then 67, he had left an idyllic retirement in Montana to roll up his sleeves and fix it.

Schulman had at first been reluctant to take the top job, turning down the offer twice. But he also felt a sense of responsibility to its customers, shareholders, and employees. Should the board have acted sooner? “Yes, we probably should have,” he concedes. Ultimately, his wife persuaded him that he could make a difference. “I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude,” he says, but adds that now he’s “absolutely loving it.”

He also came in determined to dismantle the bureaucracy that had made even simple decisions needlessly complicated. The company, he says, had become “a big lumbering giant that had fallen behind.” In some cases, approving a decision required 35 signatures.

Verizon’s competitive troubles were mounting, too. In 2024, T-Mobile added a net 3.1 million postpaid phone lines and AT&T added 1.65 million; Verizon added less than 900,000. In the first three quarters of 2025, Verizon’s consumer business lost a net 414,000 postpaid phone lines, including 356,000 in the first quarter alone. Verizon remains the largest U.S. wireless carrier, generating billions in profits. But as its peers have narrowed the gap in network quality, the advantage that once let Verizon command a premium is becoming a baseline expectation for any major wireless carrier.

As if Verizon’s existing challenges weren’t daunting enough, Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, purchased an $8 billion portfolio of low-band cellular spectrum licenses in October, a move that lays the groundwork to compete more directly with traditional wireless giants.

For years, Verizon summed up its pitch to American consumers in a familiar TV refrain: “Can you hear me now? Good.” The commercials featured a bespectacled Verizon employee, played by actor Paul Marcarelli, roaming the country and testing his service in remote locations. The catchphrase became a cultural touchstone, helping cement Verizon’s reputation for network reliability.

But over time, that advantage became harder to monetize as network coverage became less of a differentiator and consumers increasingly judged carriers on the overall customer experience, from their monthly bills to the deals available when they needed a new phone. “Customers don’t want to pay for a great network; that’s the expectation,” says Kevin Zavaglia, Verizon’s chief commercial officer for sales and service. (Adding insult to injury, Marcarelli resurfaced in 2016 as pitchman for rival Sprint, this time touting its network.)

Just over a year into Schulman’s tenure, Verizon is showing early signs of a turnaround. In the third quarter, it gained a net 406,000 phone lines, compared with just 44,000 a year earlier, its strongest third-quarter showing in five years. It also added 137,000 customer accounts, its best quarterly performance in more than a decade, even as the company slashed spending on promotional offers by 41%.

One tendency he encountered at Verizon was managers setting goals they were confident they could meet, then treating hitting those targets as success. Schulman recalls a manager proudly presenting a plan to raise a sales closing rate from 15% to 25%. “So, are you saying at the end of that, we are losing 75% of the time?” Schulman asked incredulously.

He’s pushing executives to set more ambitious goals, even if that means missing some targets, rather than consistently meeting easy ones. “Anytime the pace of change external is greater than the pace of change internal,” he says, “you’re falling behind.”

Tony Skiadas, Verizon’s chief financial officer, described how the company’s pricing strategy had become a costly cycle. Verizon had raised prices, contributing to customer defections, then spent heavily on promotions to win customers back. “We’ve seen that movie before over the years, and we know how it ends,” he says.

Roxanne Austin, a Verizon director, recalls watching the company finish third among the major wireless carriers for 20 consecutive quarters, losing customers and market share while management kept prioritizing network infrastructure over customers’ changing needs. “I’m like, ‘Guys, we’ve got to pay attention. Something’s happening,’ ” she remembers thinking. “Our playbook didn’t change for five years.” (Hans Vestberg, Verizon’s CEO from 2018 to 2025, declined to comment.)

Austin likens the scale and urgency of Schulman’s turnaround task to “turning an ocean liner at the speed of a race car.” And given the complexity of telecommunications, she adds, he must somehow “land that ocean liner on the moon, too.”

After stepping down as PayPal’s CEO in 2023 after nearly a decade at the helm, Schulman had settled happily into retirement on a Montana ranch. He rode horses daily, helped herd the couple’s roughly 900 head of cattle, and spent time with his children. Schulman, who was originally from New Jersey but had worn cowboy boots since eighth grade, finally had the lifestyle to match his footwear. “I did not miss the CEO job at all,” he says. Now, back on an executive’s grueling schedule, Schulman wants to make every hour count.

The mantra for the company’s new era under Schulman is familiar corporate gospel: Put customers first. But living up to it will require fundamental shifts at Verizon, including sacrificing some short-term revenue to rebuild customer trust. One of Schulman’s early decisions was to cancel a planned price increase. Verizon is also looking to compete more aggressively for customers with deals like the new Simplicity offering, which lowers the starting monthly price for a single line from $65 to as low as $30. And to reduce churn, it is offering incentives for customers to bundle cell phone service with home internet, including its Fios service.

Schulman made steep cost cuts, including the promised layoffs: A month after his appointment Verizon cut roughly 13,000 jobs, or about 13% of the workforce. Verizon had conducted smaller rounds of layoffs before, but Schulman wanted to send a stronger signal. “I really needed to show that this was different,” he says. “That I was very serious about the change that was going to happen.”

Schulman has set uncompromising expectations. He demands intensity, long hours, and a willingness to make difficult decisions. He expects managers to know their businesses inside out and answer questions on the spot. In meetings, when executives suggest taking a discussion offline, he challenges them: “Why would we take it offline? Like, we’re all here.”

Schulman readily describes himself as competitive and exacting of his employees, and he accepts that some may find his leadership style too demanding and leave. “And I’m okay with it, one way or another,” he says. As he puts it, “Heaven and hell are the same place. It’s just heaven for some and hell for others.”

The growing demand for infrastructure to support artificial intelligence offers new opportunities for Verizon, particularly in providing the high-capacity fiber networks connecting data centers. Verizon has signed agreements with Google, Amazon Web Services, and others worth billions, Schulman says.

AI is also helping improve systems within Verizon—for example, tools that help customer service employees quickly find information about plans, products, and policies. Zavaglia says AI has cut about six minutes from the in-store phone buying process.

As for Musk’s threat to challenge the incumbents in the mobile business, Schulman says he takes SpaceX’s ambitions “quite seriously.” But he estimates that building a network to rival Verizon’s would could take four to six years and cost some $300 billion. SpaceX also has other businesses competing for investment and attention, he points out. And even if Musk commits the resources, Schulman argues, he could end up with a network much like Verizon’s, without a significant cost advantage.

“Frankly, at that point, I welcome the opportunity to compete against them,” Schulman said during Verizon’s quarterly earnings call in October. “It’s very hard to throw a punch against something that doesn’t exist. But once they come into the market, we will be ferociously competitive.”

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

Ruth Umoh is the C-suite and Leadership editor at Fortune. She also authors Fortune’s Next to Lead newsletter.

#5437. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5436. U.S. and China are launching a superintelligence risk dialogue ahead of Trump-Xi talks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the channel will let either side alert the other to serious incidents involving its models

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a new dialogue with China on superintelligence on Tuesday, days before President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping. Bessent spoke at a National Committee on U.S.-China Relations event in New York.

Bessent said the dialogue, which began at Trump's direction, is meant to address risks both countries face and to keep either side from misreading the other's systems. He said the two sides anticipate sharing their approaches to vetting advanced models prior to launch, as well as to making sure human judgment stays in charge of the technology.

Bessent said the U.S. and China are also building a dedicated line of communication through which either nation can warn the other about grave incidents tied to its superintelligence models. He said new areas of risk management will need attention as the technology advances.

Bessent said he will join Trump in Shenzhen next week, where the two leaders are to meet before a fourth encounter in Miami. It would be their third meeting this year, after Trump's May trip to Beijing and Xi's September visit to Washington. The Shenzhen meeting falls on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Meeting on Nov. 18-19, according to CNBC.

Bessent offered no pledge to hold back progress in the technology, according to CNBC. The Trump administration has mostly pushed back on wider curbs on how AI is built, fearing that tighter rules would hand China an advantage, CNBC said. In an interview released Sunday, Trump said he does not mind guardrails but does not want the U.S. in "a deep second position" behind China, according to CNBC.

China’s Foreign Ministry dismissed calls in September to slow frontier models, according to CNBC.

Xie Feng, China's ambassador to the U.S., also spoke at the event. He said joint efforts by the two countries are "indispensable" to improving AI governance, according to Bloomberg.

The dialogue follows the first AI-focused talks between the countries' top trade negotiators, which China's Commerce Ministry confirmed on Sept. 24. Both governments had agreed at the May summit in Beijing to establish intergovernmental AI talks. Bessent said in September that the two countries had settled on creating an AI dialogue, according to Bloomberg.
