#5435. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5434. Qatar signals progress on Iran deal, but Gulf fears persist

Qatar continued its diplomatic push to broker an end to the U.S.-Iran war this week, but prospects of a breakthrough remain uncertain.

On Tuesday, a Qatari government spokesperson said that Monday’s closed-door talks between the U.S. and Iran were “focused on making progress”, but that the timeline for a potential agreement remained unclear.

“We cannot say how close or how far away an agreement is,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of the foreign ministry’s media and communication department, told a weekly briefing in Doha.

His remarks followed those of Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani who described his White House meeting on Monday with U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as “positive”.

Emerging from the latest round of shuttle diplomacy, Al Thani said he was “Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.” Before Al Thani’s visit to Washington, Qatari officials had held talks in Tehran as well as consultations with other regional governments.

On Tuesday, Al Thani made an unscheduled stop at the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris where top European diplomats have reportedly been pressing U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to avoid any new escalation against Iran.

Trump, meanwhile, took to Truth Social to argue that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE “would prefer the status quo”, referencing both the U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on Iran’s overland trade under Operation Iron Gate. Echoing Qatar’s comments, he said: “We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this conflict” but warned that the U.S. is “locked and loaded” should there be any changes in regional developments, adding “that seems to be quite unlikely”.

Speaking at a geopolitical forum in Abu Dhabi on Monday, Anwar Gargash, diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said: “We should prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional ​order can be taken for granted.” This would require the UAE to invest in its defensive capabilities and stronger international security partners, he said.

The number of attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait peaked in October, reaching its highest monthly level since the U.S.-Iran war began, with more than 30 incidents recorded, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.

On Tuesday, GCC defence ministers approved plans to establish a joint command center in Kuwait, with member states contributing forces to strengthen military integration across the six-nation bloc.

The advanced command will form part of the existing Unified Military Command which is headquartered in Riyadh. However, the announcement offered no details on the number or composition of forces to be assigned, the command’s specific mandate or when it would become operational.

The continuing uncertainty did not deter Barclays from opening its new office in Riyadh’s financial district on Monday. It marks the U.K. lender’s return to the market after more than a decade as it seeks to expand its Gulf business. Barclays’ Asia-Pacific CEO Jaideep Khanna told Bloomberg last month that the bank was a “big believer” in the Middle East.

But ongoing Houthi attacks across Saudi Arabia mean it is far from business as usual at present. Global finance firms based in Riyadh’s financial district have been allowing staff to work from home for the last month, while ongoing travel restrictions continue to create additional challenges for those commuting from nearby Gulf hubs, as well as for global executives flying directly into the kingdom.

Emirates Group's profits fell 66% for the April to September period as the U.S.-Iran war reduced passenger demand and drove up global jet fuel costs.

The Dubai-headquartered airline made a profit before tax of AED 4.1bn ($1.1bn) in the first half of its 2026-27 financial year, compared with the AED12.2bn ($3.32 billion) it made in the same period last year.

The airline carried 21.8 million passengers, 22% fewer than a year earlier while available seat kilometers—the industry's ​standard measure of passenger-carrying capacity—fell 17%.

Cargo operations helped to cushion the decline, with Emirates SkyCargo transporting 1.2 million tons over the six-month period. While this represented a 1% decline year-on-year, it still translated to a 52% increase in revenue, as the war prompted more shipping companies to turn to air transport.

Emirates fuel price risk management strategy significantly offset the impact of a 60% jump in fuel prices. Gains of AED 7.1bn ($1.9bn) from fuel hedging cut the net increase in costs to 13% but fuel remains the largest component of the airline’s operating cost at 34%.

Emirates had restored operations across 91% of its network by the end of September, serving 150 airports in 78 countries and territories. At the end of March, it was flying at 58% of its passenger capacity to 122 destinations in 65 countries.

While other airlines’ operations have been affected by regional airspace restrictions and travel advisories, Emirates has stepped in to meet passenger demand.

In total, 11 airlines, including some of Emirates’ key rivals, currently maintain suspensions on flights to Dubai. Last week, British Airways resumed direct flights to Dubai after an eight-month suspension.

The great and the good of the telecommunications industry gathered in Doha this week to attend the second Gulf annual Mobile World Congress.

The event opened with a call to action from H.E. Mohammed bin Ali al-Mannai, Qatar’s minister of communications and information technology, to align global industry standards and bridge the Middle East and Africa’s connectivity gap.

Almost half (48%) of MENA’s population used mobile internet in 2025, according to a GSMA report released at MWC Doha. However, 49% remained offline despite living within coverage.

Mobile connectivity is quickly becoming a core pillar of the region’s economic diversification, with the Gulf being home to some of the world’s most advanced 5G markets.

Mobile technologies and services, which generated $380 billion of economic value across MENA in 2025, equivalent to 5.8% of regional GDP, are forecast to reach $470 billion by 2030.

Meanwhile, 5G is expected to account for 40% of regional connections by 2030, up from 9% in 2025, as mobile operators invest a forecast $88.9 billion over the five-year period.

In just under a decade, the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) has become a hub for innovation and is now home to more than 2,000 AI, fintech, and technology companies—a sizeable leap from just 11 startups that joined its accelerator in 2017.

FinTech Hive is both the region’s first and largest financial technology accelerator and has played a key role in modernizing the emirate’s financial sector.

HSBC, BNP Paribas, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, Standard Chartered, Visa, Ripple and Network International, were among the major names who attended Dubai Future Finance Week last week, a five-day event that incorporated the two-day Dubai FinTech Summit.

DIFC announced a strategic partnership with Japan’s Mizuho Financial Group to support the international expansion of Japanese startups and deepen economic ties between the UAE and Japan. The partnership will give up to 6,000 Mizuho startup clients access to DIFC’s Innovation Hub.

DIFC also announced plans for a Dubai Fintech Stack to support founders with payments, onboarding, risk, financial security and AI integration.

Speaking as part of a headline session at Dubai FinTech Summit, Noel Quinn, chair of the wealth manager Julius Baer and former group CEO of HSBC, predicted that AI is set to become an integral part of every bank’s technology stack, particularly in monitoring payments for potential money laundering and sanctions violations. Julius Baer was the first organisation to be licensed to operate in the DIFC after the free zone was established in 2004 and has maintained a presence there ever since.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have effectively imposed their own shipping controls in the Red Sea through an often-overlooked application system for captains seeking transit clearances. The process is surprisingly simple: email the rebels. This Wall Street Journal investigative piece does a deep dive into how, in early 2024, the Houthis set up the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, an administrative body responsible for processing shipping applications and communicating the group’s sanctions. The Houthi militants, if they choose to reply, will typically do so within 24 hours, according to crew members and emails seen by the Journal. It provides an example from September when the Houthis approved passage for the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, a Chinese containership, which sailed through the Red Sea without incident.

#5433. Will AI change banking more in the next five years than the past 30? UAE lenders think so

Banking in the UAE is approaching an inflection point as AI begins to reshape everything from customer service and compliance to cybersecurity and internal operations.

Developments highlighted at last week’s Dubai FinTech Summit 2026 suggest that the country’s largest lenders are no longer simply experimenting with AI but preparing to make it a fundamental part of how they operate.

Emirates NBD, Dubai’s largest lender by assets, shared how it has more than 150 AI initiatives underway, with 65 already in production.

The bank, which is majority government-owned, has been aggressively scaling its digital transformation by committing approximately 50% of its technology budget to AI.

In June, Emirates NBD was ranked first in the Evident AI Index for Banks – Middle East & Africa which assesses how banks across these regions are deploying AI and adapting their operations to the technology’s transformative impact.

The survey carried out by Evident, a London-based market intelligence firm, comprised more than 100 companies, including insurers and payment processors.

It noted that Emirates NBD “explicitly” links AI to enterprise productivity, operational modernisation and the UAE’s national AI agenda.

The bank plans to integrate OpenAI’s models across its operations to enhance customer experiences, strengthen risk management and financial crime prevention through advanced analytics, automate processes and boost employee productivity.

“Banking will transform more in the next five years than it transformed in the last 30 years,” said Miguel Rio-Tinto, Emirates NBD’s Group Chief Digital and Information Officer.

“Generative AI and advanced frontier models are so powerful that they are opening up new possibilities for automation in banking, enabling capabilities that were previously out of reach across customer service, internal processes and employee support. I believe AI will be the key determinant in shaping the competitive landscape of the future.”

Cybersecurity is the area where Rio-Tinto anticipates the most significant transformation. As advanced AI models become increasingly capable of identifying software vulnerabilities, the number of critical security flaws the bank must evaluate has surged from approximately 1,000 per month in early 2025 to around 15,000 last month.

To address this growing challenge, Emirates NBD is adopting the same technology defensively, leveraging a frontier OpenAI model to test and identify weaknesses in its own systems.

The rapid digital transformation taking place across the region has increased its exposure to cyberattacks while the need to strengthen operational resilience across the Gulf has become increasingly pressing since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on February 28.

In the UAE, daily attempted cyberattacks reportedly surged from around 200,000 to as many as 700,000 amid the escalating geopolitical tensions.

In July, the UAE successfully thwarted a series of sophisticated cyberattacks targeting its financial sector that sought to compromise digital systems and technical infrastructure through phishing campaigns and malicious software.

The UAE’s Cyber Security Council warned that cybercriminals are increasingly harnessing AI to devise more sophisticated attack methods.

While cybersecurity is emerging as a critical area where AI can make a difference, UAE lenders are looking to deploy the technology across a broad range of functions, with Commercial Bank of Dubai (CBD) unveiling a series of strategic technology partnerships at the summit.

Collaborations with Microsoft, Silent Eight, and Comarch AI Wealth will, respectively, support wider AI adoption, strengthen AI-powered compliance and risk management, and further develop the bank’s digital wealth platform and investment offerings.

CBD also joined forces with Zamp to leverage intelligent automation and signed strategic agreements with Harvey, Sirion, and Flank to improve its legal and governance infrastructure.

“We are moving away from traditional AI applications towards adopting agentic AI, which is creating opportunities to rethink and redesign existing business processes,” said Thomas Cherian, Commercial Bank of Dubai’s chief technology and services officer.

“This will help us accelerate service delivery and provide superior customer experiences. Agentic AI is enabling us to move towards much more intelligent banking which is safer and more secure for our customers, highlighting technology’s growing role today as a strategic enabler for banks.”

Unlike conventional generative AI, agentic AI can make decisions and execute tasks autonomously with minimal human intervention.

Cherian estimates that AI agents could handle 55% to 60% of operational tasks, with human oversight retained to approve outcomes. CBD also aims to retain ownership of the agents it develops and the intellectual property behind them.

The UAE has recently placed agentic AI at the top of its technology agenda. In April this year, the UAE government launched a major national initiative to transition 50% of all federal government operations, services, and tasks to agentic AI systems by 2028.

The following month, Dubai announced a two-year action plan to accelerate the adoption of the technology across the emirate’s private sector, aiming to secure a “competitive edge” in the future global economy.

With the government’s ambitious targets for agentic AI adoption and banks committing significant resources to the technology, the UAE’s financial sector looks poised for a fundamental transformation.

#5432. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5431. Finland is allowing Tesla's assisted driving system before E.U. approval

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Traficom recognized the Dutch provisional type-approval, while final E.U.-wide approval still needs a committee vote

Finland has cleared Tesla $TSLA’s Assisted Driving system for its roads, getting out in front of an EU-wide ruling that is anticipated in the winter months.

The Finnish Transport and Communications Agency, known as Traficom, recognized the provisional type-approval that regulators in the Netherlands issued on Tuesday, the agency said. Tesla can start offering the system to its customers in Finland with immediate effect.

Final approval across the EU requires a successful vote in the European Commission’s Technical Committee – Motor Vehicles, Traficom said. Approval takes effect about three weeks after a successful vote. Traficom said national recognition does not bind Finland in that vote, and the country will follow discussions among member states on the system’s features before deciding its position.

Traficom said it moved ahead of the EU process because of changes Tesla has made to the system. It also said earlier recognition gives Finnish Tesla users time to get used to the system ahead of the harshest winter driving conditions.

"The system's design and approval assessment have taken winter conditions into account, but its operation may be subject to various limitations if the cameras become covered in snow, slush or other dirt, or if traffic conditions become more challenging than usual," said Jukka Juhola, a senior specialist at Traficom.

The most visible change is the name. The system was called FSD (Supervised), short for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), and references to self-driving have been removed. The new name appears in Finnish- and Swedish-language marketing and user guidance materials. Tesla's choice of name has drawn criticism from regulators, safety groups and some of its own customers, who say it implies full autonomy, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla also changed the system's speed settings. Drivers can no longer encourage the system to keep an unnecessarily high speed above the limit. Settings that allow speeding reset to the default, with no deviation from the speed limit, each time the vehicle restarts. The information shown to drivers about the speed settings the system has selected has been expanded and clarified.

Traficom expects further changes before EU-wide approval. Those changes will not significantly affect how the system is used but will help drivers stay alert, the agency said.

Traficom stressed that the driver remains fully responsible for driving, even when the experience resembles that of a self-driving car. Drivers must monitor the system throughout the trip and be ready to steer, brake or accelerate without waiting for a request from the system.

"Drivers must still be aware of the speed limit and comply with it," Juhola said. "It is always the driver who receives the fine for speeding."

Installing the system does not require a modification inspection for vehicles that have not been modified, Traficom said. Unusual tire sizes or suspension lowering kits are examples of changes that would require one.

#5430. ByteDance is planning an AI agent similar to Meta's Muse within weeks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Co-founder Zhang Yiming told AI staff that competing with Anthropic and OpenAI at the cutting edge will take at least until 2029 or 2030

ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, is preparing to launch an AI agent comparable to Meta $META Platforms' Muse within the next few weeks, according to Bloomberg. The company hopes the launch will build on its advantage in AI video and help close the gap with leading American labs in as little as three years, Bloomberg said.

Co-founder Zhang Yiming described the plan to the company's AI team at an all-hands meeting, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed people familiar with the matter. Zhang said ByteDance is capable of challenging Anthropic and OpenAI at the frontier, but he warned that getting there would mean waiting until 2029 or 2030 at the earliest.

Meta introduced Muse in September. It talks with users by voice, appears on screen as an animated character, and assists them in completing a range of chores, while Meta is rolling it out on its smart glasses and on a forthcoming Muse Charm device, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg said it remains unknown if ByteDance intends to pair its agent with a physical device.

Zhang, 43, named data as a top concern. He said the training datasets behind ByteDance's Seed large language models are orders of magnitude smaller than what frontier rivals use, according to Bloomberg.

Zhang again argued that ByteDance should steer clear of distillation, which means teaching a compact model with what a bigger one produces, and keep its attention on long-range goals, according to Bloomberg. White House officials and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have faulted Chinese rivals including Alibaba, Moonshot AI and Z.ai for building on top American models through distillation.

Seed stands alone among China's top AI players in having neither produced a language model that ranks among the world's best on benchmarks nor made its weights accessible to outside developers, according to Bloomberg. The Seed 2.1 update in June was ByteDance's last major language model release.

Video is the area where ByteDance holds a meaningful lead, according to Bloomberg. Its Seedance models stepped in after OpenAI discontinued Sora, and the company intends to commit up to $70 billion to turn Seedance into the leading video AI platform in China.

ByteDance secured a $29.6 billion loan in September from close to three dozen banks, with proceeds earmarked for AI initiatives outside China, including data centers under development in Southeast Asia. The three-year facility had no collateral.

The Seed team employs around 1,000 people in research and engineering roles and is headed by Wu Yonghui, whom Zhang recruited away from Google $GOOGL DeepMind in 2025, according to Bloomberg. In October, Seed became the first of China's big AI labs to launch its own separate unit for safety and alignment, Bloomberg said.

A ByteDance spokesperson did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.

#5429. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5428. Current price of oil as of November 11, 2026

At 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $95.72 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s an increase of $2.74 since yesterday morning and roughly $30 more than at this time last year.

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted.

It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating.

Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas.

Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

Joseph is a staff writer on Fortune's personal finance commerce team. He's covered personal finance since 2016, previously serving as a reporter and editor at sites like Business Insider and The Points Guy. He has also contributed to major outlets such as AP News, CNN, Newsweek, and many more.

#5427. The next Congress could be more productive than you expect. Here’s what that means for your company

David Meadvin is CEO of One Strategy Group, a firm that advises CEOs and companies on reputation, risk, and navigating complexity. He was previously a speechwriter for Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid.

When I was Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid’s speechwriter, there were very few nail-biter votes. Hanging around the cloakroom, 99 percent of the time we could predict the exact outcome of a vote before the roll call began.

That’s how we’re all trained to think about Washington now. We’ve been through years of gridlock, and our pattern recognition-obsessed brains assume there will be more. The fundamentals of a divided federal government suggest the same: Democrats control both chambers, President Trump holds the veto pen, overcoming a filibuster still requires 60 votes, and overturning a veto requires 67.

But the 2026 election scrambled the incentives that have kept Washington gridlocked for so long.

That means things could get a little weird next year.

To understand this shift, start with the next map. In 2028, 18 Republican senators are up for re-election, and seven of them represent states that either elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2026 or came within three points of doing so.

Sen. Ashley Moody held her Florida seat by under three points, and she faces voters again in two years. Sen. John Kennedy just watched Louisiana nearly elect its first Democratic senator since 2008. Sens. Jerry Moran, Tim Scott and Ted Budd represent states where Democrats won Senate races this year. So will whoever runs for Sen. Chuck Grassley’s seat in Iowa.

The years 2016 to 2026 will forever be remembered as the MAGA decade. During this period, the most existential fear keeping Republicans up at night was a primary challenge to their right with Trump support. This spring, Trump helped push out Bill Cassidy in Louisiana and John Cornyn in Texas. They were the latest in a long string of Republican casualties when their loyalty to the president was questioned.

Look at what happened to the nominees who replaced Cassidy and Cornyn. Ken Paxton lost Texas by 12 points. Julia Letlow, Trump’s pick in Louisiana, held the seat by less than two. Republicans lost general elections in places like South Carolina and (probably) Mississippi that no one would have imagined would host a competitive general election. Even Montana, one of the most Republican states in the nation, might have elected a Democratic senator if the Democratic nominee and a stronger independent candidate hadn’t split votes.

For the last decade, Republican senators had more reason to fear losing a primary than losing a general election. That math no longer holds. In almost any state, winning the primary in 2028 will be just half the battle. There will be very few obviously safe Republican Senate seats in America next cycle, especially if cost of living issues don’t dramatically improve in the next two years.

There are plenty of explanations for the Democratic wave, but the Republican Party’s failure to deliver on its economic populist promises has to be near the top of the list. If you’re wondering which issues might see strange bedfellows during the 2027 legislative session, start there.

We’re already seeing the shift. Four days after the election, Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, one of Trump’s most loyal allies in the Senate, went on Fox News and accused people inside the Trump administration of serving special interests. When Trump made clear he took it personally, Johnson widened his complaint to “deep state” actors in every administration. But he made the break first and softened it second, and his core complaint was that corporations have become too close to the agencies that regulate them. For a conservative like Johnson facing the prospect of an uphill re-election fight if he runs again, aligning himself with economic populism won’t be optional.

Heading into 2028, Republicans facing re-election need to show voters at home that they can do something about the cost of living. In the NBC News exit poll, nearly 90 percent of voters said they were concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and health care. Those voters will remember who helped and who stood in the way.

Don’t roll your eyes. I’m not suggesting that Republicans will sign on to signature Democratic priorities. But on legislation that addresses voters’ economic concerns – and isn’t indelibly aligned with the Democratic Party – we could see filibuster-proof and even veto-proof majorities emerge.

We know where to find these types of coalitions. Just this past summer, the Senate passed a major housing bill by an 85-5 vote; it became law even though Trump refused to sign it. An issue like data centers defies obvious partisan labels, and legislation to prevent them from passing costs onto local communities came close to passing this fall (Democrats voted no because they thought the bill didn’t go far enough; a toothier version could well pass next year). Other issues with broad appeal could include permitting reform and health insurance premiums.

Nothing will test these new coalitions more than tariffs. We could see legislation restoring Congress’s authority over tariffs. Will all but the safest Republicans really side with the White House on this one? Overriding a presidential veto would take two-thirds of both chambers. In the Senate, if Democrats end up with 56 seats, that means 11 Republicans. In the House, it would take about 30, and there are roughly 40 House Republicans who won this year by five points or less. A year ago those numbers would have sounded absurd. With seven clearly vulnerable Republican senators and several others who have already backed giving Congress the final word on trade, it is no longer out of the question.

This is not just a game of political prognostication. CEOs and their companies who agree that there’s a reasonable chance of big legislation moving with bipartisan support next year need to plan for it. Some of the coalitions that form will move on issues companies have wanted for years, like permitting. Others will form against particular industries. Tech companies that assumed the data center buildout would go unchallenged should expect major headaches, and likely far higher costs than they’ve planned.

Corporate public affairs executives who rely on the old assumptions about Washington may find themselves badly unprepared for 2027. CEOs, beware of anyone on your team who confidently breaks down expected voting patterns and legislative agendas based on how things always go. One of my favorite quotes, from Dwight Eisenhower, is “plans are useless, planning is everything.” Now’s the time to plan.

#5426. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5425. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5424. Meet Rox, the $1.3 billion AI sales startup betting it can take on Salesforce

Morgan Chittum here. For decades, enterprise software giants like Salesforce have powered the workflows that keep the world’s biggest businesses running. Rox cofounder Ishan Mukherjee is betting on a future that no longer needs them.

The AI sales startup has raised $100 million in Series B funding at a $1.3 billion valuation, Rox exclusively told Fortune. General Catalyst and March Capital co-led the round, with Sequoia and GV returning and Prosperity7 joining as a new investor.

The pitch: Customer relationship management software shouldn’t just store information. It should put it to work. With Rox, AI agents research customer accounts, recommend who to prioritize, and prepare outreach for clients. Basically, it gives salespeople less administrative work and more time with clients.

Mukherjee’s conviction comes from experience. Before Rox, he started Pixie Labs, which New Relic acquired for roughly $150 million in 2020, and became New Relic’s chief growth officer.

“While running a public company through COVID, I deeply understood that every business relies on Salesforce specifically and their CRM to run their business. That was not the futureproof approach as AI was about to hit scale,” Mukherjee said.

“There are going to be autonomous agents that do customer-facing commercial work across large parts of the economy, not just tech companies,” he added. “And do we think Salesforce is the right partner to help CEOs in the C-suite to actually transform their businesses? I came out of an experience where it was not true.”

He also saw an opening as massive companies like Nvidia and Intel moved customer data out of Salesforce and into their own environments. “What that means is the world’s largest in-app application company, which is Salesforce, was becoming less of a moat, less entrenched,” Mukherjee added.

But how do they plan to take on Salesforce, a company with a $172 billion market cap? Mukherjee pointed to the founding team’s experience developing cutting edge tech. Rox’s cofounders include Shriram Sridharan, a founding member of AWS’s Amazon Aurora database service; former Google employee Diogo Ribeiro; and Stanford AI Lab professor Christopher Ré. Mukherjee, himself, was a product lead for Apple’s Siri Knowledge Graph.

That was a key reason General Catalyst invested pre-product, and pre-revenue, back in 2024, partner Marc Bhargava said, describing Rox as “a talent magnet.”

But talent alone won’t unseat an enterprise software behemoth: “For a long time there’s been a graveyard of companies that said ‘I’m taking on ServiceNow or Workday. I’m taking on Salesforce,’” Bhargava told Fortune. Sticky customer relationships and access to capital have kept those incumbents in control, he said. “But AI is a moment in time to displace many of them.” Those same fears have rattled Wall Street in 2026, at times sending software tumbling in what became known as the “SaaSpocalypse.”

Rox’s argument: AI-native startups can build around agents from the start, rather than retrofit them into older software. “It’s like you have a house and you just throw in one more floor, versus from the beginning you decided it was going to be a four-floor home,” Bhargava added. “It’s a huge opportunity for people to start fresh with a fresh code base built around [large language models]…Those products are ultimately better.”

To be sure, the incumbents aren’t easy targets. Salesforce generated $41.5 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and says it has worked with more than 150,000 companies. ServiceNow, meanwhile, ended its latest quarter with 680 customers with more than $5 million each in annual contract value.

Meanwhile, Rox’s early customers include high-profile firms like Ramp, New Relic, Trafigura, MongoDB, Groq, and America’s Auto Auction, to name a few. The startup also says its annual recurring revenue grew more than tenfold since its first year after launch. The fresh capital will fund more AI research and product development. Rox plans to expand its U.S. sales, marketing, and commercial team fivefold next year.

“Us in venture, our whole thing is to back the Davids against the Goliaths,” Bhargava said, “And we think that this will happen here.”

#5423. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5422. Think Bigger!! Schwartz Calls for Higher XRP Price as 37 European Banks Embrace Ripple

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

David Schwartz has delivered a fresh bullish message to frustrated XRP holders, saying that a higher price could make the network more efficient. The Ripple CTO believes XRP has more to gain from successful XRP Ledger adoption than its current market valuation.

“The higher the price, the better,” Schwartz wrote in response to a community member questioning whether XRP could support large payment volumes. He explained that higher valuations could make liquidity more cost-effective while reducing slippage during transactions.

The higher the price, the better. A higher price would tend to mean liquidity is more cost-effective and slippage is less.

His comments arrive as XRP trades near $1.10, leaving investors frustrated after another significant market correction. However, developments across Europe’s banking sector are giving the long-term adoption argument fresh momentum.

Schwartz’s latest comments address one of the biggest questions surrounding XRP’s investment thesis: whether the token can capture value as the XRP Ledger expands.

A higher XRP price could make the asset more practical for institutions transferring substantial amounts of money. Each token would represent greater value, potentially reducing the amount of XRP needed for large settlements.

More importantly, deeper liquidity could allow institutions to execute larger transactions without moving the market. That makes XRP’s potential role as a bridge asset particularly interesting for cross-border payments.

Schwartz also offered a strong defense of XRP’s long-term value proposition.

I really do think it's hard to believe we will end up in a world where XRPL is successful but XRP fails to capture a good fraction of that value.

That statement gives XRP holders a bigger reason to watch network adoption beyond daily price movements. Schwartz also acknowledged that XRP’s price currently follows broader cryptocurrency market conditions more closely than developments specific to Ripple and the XRP Ledger.

Nevertheless, his comments reinforce the argument that successful network adoption could eventually benefit the underlying token.

The institutional side of the story is becoming increasingly interesting as European banks prepare to expand blockchain-based financial services.

Qivalis, a consortium of 37 European financial institutions across 15 countries, is preparing to introduce a regulated euro-denominated stablecoin.

The initiative aims to establish a shared digital euro infrastructure for payments and settlements. It could also help European banks compete with dollar-backed stablecoins dominating the global market.

The consortium received Electronic Money Institution authorization from the Dutch central bank in October 2026, bringing its planned stablecoin closer to commercial launch.

Two particularly interesting members are BBVA and DZ BANK, both of which have existing relationships with Ripple’s institutional custody business.

BBVA announced an agreement with Ripple in September 2025 to use Ripple Custody technology for its digital asset services. DZ BANK has also worked with Ripple on institutional digital asset custody infrastructure.

Their participation in Qivalis highlights how established European banks are increasingly exploring blockchain-based financial products.

The immediate market picture remains challenging, but derivatives data offers an interesting contrast. XRP is trading under $1.10, following a sharp correction that pushed the token toward its lowest levels since August.

Binance’s XRP cumulative volume delta recently turned negative, indicating that aggressive market selling exceeded buying activity. This suggests buyers have yet to absorb the latest wave of selling pressure.

Liquidations have also weighed on sentiment. XRP recorded approximately $26 million in liquidations across seven exchanges on November 9, with long positions accounting for 98.4% of the total. Meanwhile, US spot XRP ETFs recorded approximately $10.4 million in net outflows on November 9.

However, these figures do not erase the longer-term institutional developments surrounding Ripple. The growing demand for regulated digital asset infrastructure could create opportunities for XRP as financial institutions explore more efficient ways to move value.

Schwartz’s argument is ultimately about looking beyond the token’s immediate market performance. If the XRP Ledger captures a meaningful share of institutional payments and settlement activity, XRP could become increasingly important as a liquidity asset.

#5421. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”
